chunk_findings.detail: The attribute line `*/schema.json -diff linguist-vendored` (and `LICENSE -diff`) sets only `-diff`; it does not set `-text`. `-diff` merely tells diff to treat the path as binary — it leaves the `text` attribute *unspecified*, so git still auto-detects these JSON/LICENSE files as text and applies end-of-line conversion on checkout. On a Windows clone with the Git for Windows default `core.autocrlf=true` (or any `core.eol=crlf` configuration), git rewrites LF to CRLF in the working tree, so the bytes on disk are not the bytes in the blob. The manifest hashes and `tests/test_mcp_protocol_conformance.py` hash the on-disk files, so the sha256 comparison fails for all five revisions even though nothing upstream changed — the exact guarantee the file's own comment claims ("byte for byte, held to their sha256"). To actually hold that guarantee the pattern needs `-text` (i.e. `binary` / `-diff -merge -text`), not just `-diff`.

chunk_findings.detail: The "forged" token is produced by rewriting the last two characters of the genuine tag to `"AA"`. When the genuine tag already ends in `AA` (a hex digest under a random per-process key hits this about once in 256 runs; base64url similar order of magnitude), `forged` is byte-identical to `token`. The server then correctly serves the real state, `srv.handle(_retry(params, forged))` returns a *result*, and `reply["error"]["code"]` raises `KeyError` inside `assert reply["error"]["code"] == -32602`. So this merge-gating conformance test fails spuriously for a state that is not forged at all. The same construction is used for no other property (format, separator, length), so the "tampered token is refused" contract is only exercised on the branch where the mutation happens to change something. A deterministic mutation (e.g. flip the first tag character to a different symbol, or assert `forged != token` before presenting it) is needed for the test to be reliable.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_protocol_conformance.py `forged = f"{body}.{tag[:-2]}AA"` (in `test_a_state_this_server_did_not_issue_is_refused`)

chunk_findings.detail: The test's stated purpose is that the retry is "verified" and that "the server answers the retry like any modern call", but the only check on the server's handling is `check_reply(rev, "tools/call", M.Server(repo, agent="conformance").handle(retry))`, and `check_reply` also accepts an *error* envelope (it validates `JSONRPCErrorResponse` and returns). Concretely: if the freshly constructed `M.Server` refused the state (e.g. a state key not shared with the process that called `P.input_required`, or a binding on agent/tool that the retry fails), `handle` would return `{"error": {"code": -32602, ...}}`, the reply would still conform to the schema, and this test would pass while claiming the retry was served. The genuinely-issued-token acceptance is only asserted in `test_a_state_this_server_did_not_issue_is_refused` (`assert "result" in srv.handle(_retry(params, token))`), so the end-to-end MRTR path through a server that did not issue the state is not actually pinned by the test that names it.

chunk_findings.detail: `round_trip` treats "MAC verifies" as "payload is a well-formed state": after `hmac.compare_digest(mac, _mac(raw))` it does `payload = json.loads(raw)` and then `payload["b"]`, `payload["x"]`, `payload["s"]` with no type check. The MAC-valid preimages are not secret in the way the code assumes: the token handed to the client is `_b64(raw) + "." + _b64(_mac(raw))`, and `raw` contains `"b": _b64(_mac(binding_bytes))`, so the client learns the MAC *of the binding preimage* `X = json.dumps([method, {"arguments":…, "name":…, "uri":…}, who], sort_keys=True, separators=(",",":"), default=str)` — and it knows `X` exactly, because every field in it is taken from the request the client itself sent. So after any legitimate `InputRequiredResult` (e.g. a `tools/call` that asked for elicitation), the client can send the retry `requestState = _b64(X) + "." + <the `b` value from its own decoded token>`. In `round_trip`: `token.count(".") == 1` ✓, `_unb64(body)` decodes to `X`, `_unb64(tag)` equals `_mac(X)` so `compare_digest` **passes** ✓, and then `json.loads(X)` is a JSON *array*, so `payload["b"]` raises `TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not str`. `modern_check` wraps `round_trip` in `try: … except ValueError as exc`, and `TypeError` is not a `ValueError`, so the exception escapes `modern_check` and any caller that only distinguishes the documented `str | dict | None` returns; on a single-process stdio loop without a blanket `except`, that is a repeatable crash triggered by one malformed retry (and, at minimum, a non-JSON-RPC error/no reply for that `id`). The fix is either to validate the decoded payload inside `round_trip` (`isinstance(payload, dict)` and required keys, `isinstance(payload["x"], int)`, catching `TypeError`/`KeyError`) and raise `ValueError`, or to widen `modern_check`'s handler to `except (ValueError, TypeError, KeyError)`.

chunk_findings.detail: The rule `*/schema.json -diff linguist-vendored` clears only the diff attribute, so git's end-of-line handling for these vendored files is left to `core.autocrlf` / any higher-level `* text=auto`. `-diff` does not imply `-text` (the standard `binary` macro is `-diff -merge -text`), and the schemas are plain text JSON, so on any checkout where `core.autocrlf=true` (the default for Git for Windows) or where a root `.gitattributes` sets `text=auto`, git writes `2024-11-05/schema.json` (and the other four) out with CRLF even though the blob and the manifest hash are LF. Concretely: a Windows contributor clones, `git status` is clean, but `tests/test_mcp_protocol_conformance.py` computes `sha256` over the CRLF bytes, gets a value different from `61cea239...` in `manifest.json`, and fails — exactly the "byte for byte" property line 1 of this same file claims is enforced. The fix is to use `binary`/`-text` on these paths so checkout never rewrites them.

data.summary: mcp_protocol.input_required seals requestState as b64(raw).b64(mac(raw)) where raw carries b = mac(binding preimage X), and X is built only from what the client sent. Both MACs use one key with no domain separation, so a client presents b64(X).b64(b): the MAC verifies, json.loads(X) is a list, payload['b'] raises TypeError, which modern_check does not catch (it catches ValueError) -- an uncaught exception instead of -32602. Found by the critic review (lan-deepseek-v4.1-flash) on the unmerged branch.

The diff instead adds the three harness helpers to `KEPT_UNREFERENCED`:

```
"ddflow/services/harness.py:enable_project_servers": "B-hx-onboard-generic",
"ddflow/services/harness.py:copy_local_configs": "B-onboard-harness-stage",
"ddflow/services/harness.py:install_shell_command": "B-onboard-harness-stage",
```

Concretely: `_unreferenced_functions()` runs `_unreferenced(...)` and then drops anything whose `_kept_key` is in `KEPT_UNREFERENCED`. For a module-level `enable_project_servers` at `ddflow/services/harness.py:41`, `_kept_key("ddflow/services/harness.py:41 enable_project_servers")` yields exactly `"ddflow/services/harness.py:enable_project_servers"`, so it is filtered out regardless of whether the function was deleted in the rest of the change. The baseline `"unreferenced_functions": 6` is therefore unchanged whether those three functions exist or not, and the vulture ratchet that this change introduces will never surface them. So the step the intent describes — deleting these three truly-dead helpers — is neither performed nor detectable by the new guard; if they were in fact deleted in another part of the change, these entries are stale and the "an entry leaves this list in the change that gives it a caller" rule is violated for them (they left by deletion, not by getting a caller). Either way the allowlist and the stated intent cannot both be satisfied: the three names the change says it removes are the three it whitelists.

chunk_findings.detail: `_text` is the only place in the file where a PEP-604 union is evaluated at *runtime*. Every other union in this module (`str | None`, `DD.Answer | None`, `dict | None`, ...) sits inside an annotation and is therefore stringified by the module's `from __future__ import annotations`; the isinstance argument is a normal expression and is evaluated eagerly. On any interpreter older than 3.10 (which is exactly the range that a blanket `from __future__ import annotations` is normally there to support), `str | int | float` raises `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for |: 'type' and 'type'`. Concretely, the most common call into the new path — `def_record(repo, "rule", "r-1", {"text": "x"})`, where `title` and `body` default to `""` — reaches `_text` with `title or body` false and raises instead of returning the `def.recorded` outcome, so recording a definition that has no explicit title/body crashes. The fix is `isinstance(v, (str, int, float))`. If the project's minimum Python is 3.10+, this is a non-issue; but given that the author deliberately deferred every other union, the runtime union here is inconsistent with the rest of the file and is a real failure on the interpreters that pattern implies.

chunk_findings.detail:
The back-link from the absorbing record to the merged record is written only if the successor happens to already be in `st.defs` at the moment `def.merged` is folded, and it is never retried. The surrounding fold is explicitly designed to tolerate out-of-order arrival (`_record`'s docstring says a status change or update "created when an update or a status change arrives before its definition (a shard merged out of order)"), but `h_merged` does not honor that: `into = st.defs.get(key(rec.kind, rec.successor))` returns `None`, the `if into is not None` guard swallows it, and `merged_from` is silently lost. Given an event stream (a shard replay where the merge is ordered before the successor's definition) of

1. `def.recorded {kind:"skill", id:"A", fields:{...}}`
2. `def.merged {kind:"skill", id:"A", successor:"B"}`  (B not yet known)
3. `def.recorded {kind:"skill", id:"B", fields:{...}}`

the folded `st.defs["skill:B"].merged_from` ends up `[]` instead of `["A"]`, contradicting the handler's own contract ("Folded into `successor` ... which records that it absorbed this one"). Any consumer that resolves B's provenance from `merged_from` (the very reason the field exists) gets the wrong answer, and unlike a missing `State.defs` entry, the omission is permanent because nothing later re-derives or repairs the link.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/handlers/defs.py `h_merged`

chunk_findings.detail: The test compares `fold(evs).defs` with `fold(list(evs)).defs`, but `list(evs)` is just a copy of `evs`, so both folds receive the identical event sequence in the identical order. The assertion can never fail (for any deterministic fold) and cannot catch order-dependent folding, which is the stated purpose of this area of the fold ("Shards merge out of order: the fold never drops an event for arriving early") and of determinism. A meaningful version would fold a reordered permutation of the same events and assert `.defs` equality.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_def_records.py::test_the_fold_is_deterministic

chunk_findings.detail: `def_record` stores the caller's fields verbatim (`fields=dict(fields)`, `digest = D.digest(fields)`), and `_fields_problem` explicitly accepts JSON `null` (it only rejects non-JSON via `json.dumps(..., allow_nan=False)`). So a definition may legitimately hold a null-valued field. `def_update`, however, filters `None` out of the *combined* dict, not just out of the caller's delta. Given a definition recorded as `def_record(repo, "rule", "r1", {"a": None, "b": 1})`, a later `def_update(repo, "rule", "r1", {"b": 2})` builds `merged = {"b": 2}` and drops `a` entirely, even though the caller never mentioned `a`. The update therefore silently deletes an existing field. The two write paths disagree on what `None` means ("a value" at record time, "remove this key" at update time), and `def_update` also computes its digest from the filtered dict while `def_record` computes it from the unfiltered one, so a record containing any null field will additionally never satisfy the `digest == rec.digest` "nothing changed" check, producing spurious `def.updated` events. Either `def_record` must reject/normalize `None` the same way, or `def_update` must filter only the keys present in `fields`.

chunk_findings.detail: `def_update` accepts a `provenance` argument and forwards it to `_envelope`, but the "nothing changed" gate ignores it. The identical condition special-cases `source` yet says nothing about `provenance`, so `def_update(repo, "rule", "r1", {}, provenance={"reviewed": True})` returns `O.nothing` (exit 2) and the supplied provenance is never written, silently discarding an argument the caller supplied and making the "source is checked but provenance is not" behavior inconsistent within one function.

chunk_findings.detail: `h_merged` performs a cross-record side effect — appending the merged id to the successor's `merged_from` — by looking the successor up in `st.defs` at the moment the event is folded. This only works if the successor's record already exists. But the module explicitly supports the out-of-order case: `_record` (and its docstring "created when an update or a status change arrives before its definition (a shard merged out of order)") is built precisely so a status change can arrive before the record it targets. `h_merged` is a status change on the *source* record, yet the *successor* is never created/stubbed — it is just fetched. So given the event sequence `def.merged {kind: "rule", id: "A", successor: "B"}` followed by `def.recorded {kind: "rule", id: "B"}`, the fold creates A with status MERGED and successor B, the lookup for B returns `None`, and `B.merged_from` is never populated. The same two events in the opposite order yield `B.merged_from == ["A"]`. The fold is therefore order-dependent and silently loses the "B absorbed A" back-reference in exactly the shard-out-of-order scenario the file claims to handle; unlike `_record`, there is no re-application when B's `def.recorded` later arrives (that handler only resets status/fields and does not re-scan pending merges).

chunk_findings.detail: `assert fold(evs).defs == fold(list(evs)).defs` folds the same list twice (`list(evs)` is a same-order copy), so it is a tautology that cannot fail regardless of whether the fold is order-dependent. The test name claims to verify determinism, but the meaningful property (same result when shard events arrive in a different order) is left unverified, even though the neighboring fold test shows a `def.updated`/`def.recorded` pair is genuinely order-sensitive. Replacing the right-hand side with a reordered copy of the events would make the assertion meaningful.

chunk_findings.detail: `def_record` stores the caller's fields verbatim (`fields=dict(fields)`, `digest = D.digest(fields)`), and `_fields_problem` explicitly accepts JSON `null` (it only rejects non-JSON via `json.dumps(..., allow_nan=False)`). So a definition may legitimately hold a null-valued field. `def_update`, however, filters `None` out of the *combined* dict, not just out of the caller's delta. Given a definition recorded as `def_record(repo, "rule", "r1", {"a": None, "b": 1})`, a later `def_update(repo, "rule", "r1", {"b": 2})` builds `merged = {"b": 2}` and drops `a` entirely, even though the caller never mentioned `a`. The update therefore silently deletes an existing field. The two write paths disagree on what `None` means ("a value" at record time, "remove this key" at update time), and `def_update` also computes its digest from the filtered dict while `def_record` computes it from the unfiltered one, so a record containing any null field will additionally never satisfy the `digest == rec.digest` "nothing changed" check, producing spurious `def.updated` events. Either `def_record` must reject/normalize `None` the same way, or `def_update` must filter only the keys present in `fields`.

chunk_findings.detail: `def_update` accepts a `provenance` argument and forwards it to `_envelope`, but the "nothing changed" gate ignores it. The identical condition special-cases `source` yet says nothing about `provenance`, so `def_update(repo, "rule", "r1", {}, provenance={"reviewed": True})` returns `O.nothing` (exit 2) and the supplied provenance is never written, silently discarding an argument the caller supplied and making the "source is checked but provenance is not" behavior inconsistent within one function.

chunk_findings.detail: `h_merged` performs a cross-record side effect — appending the merged id to the successor's `merged_from` — by looking the successor up in `st.defs` at the moment the event is folded. This only works if the successor's record already exists. But the module explicitly supports the out-of-order case: `_record` (and its docstring "created when an update or a status change arrives before its definition (a shard merged out of order)") is built precisely so a status change can arrive before the record it targets. `h_merged` is a status change on the *source* record, yet the *successor* is never created/stubbed — it is just fetched. So given the event sequence `def.merged {kind: "rule", id: "A", successor: "B"}` followed by `def.recorded {kind: "rule", id: "B"}`, the fold creates A with status MERGED and successor B, the lookup for B returns `None`, and `B.merged_from` is never populated. The same two events in the opposite order yield `B.merged_from == ["A"]`. The fold is therefore order-dependent and silently loses the "B absorbed A" back-reference in exactly the shard-out-of-order scenario the file claims to handle; unlike `_record`, there is no re-application when B's `def.recorded` later arrives (that handler only resets status/fields and does not re-scan pending merges).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/handlers/defs.py: `h_merged` (the `into = st.defs.get(key(rec.kind, rec.successor))` lookup)

chunk_findings.detail: `assert fold(evs).defs == fold(list(evs)).defs` folds the same list twice (`list(evs)` is a same-order copy), so it is a tautology that cannot fail regardless of whether the fold is order-dependent. The test name claims to verify determinism, but the meaningful property (same result when shard events arrive in a different order) is left unverified, even though the neighboring fold test shows a `def.updated`/`def.recorded` pair is genuinely order-sensitive. Replacing the right-hand side with a reordered copy of the events would make the assertion meaningful.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_def_records.py:test_the_fold_is_deterministic

chunk_findings.detail: The new conjunct `and not provenance` tests truthiness of the supplied provenance instead of comparing it with what is already recorded, so it gets both directions wrong. (a) If a record already has a non-empty provenance `P`, calling `def.updated(repo, agent, kind, rid, fields=<current fields>, source=rec.source, provenance=P)` still falls through the guard (because `not P` is `False`) and emits a fresh `def.updated` event on every call, even though nothing changed: a retry/reconcile loop that re-applies the same update now appends an unbounded stream of no-op events (previously it returned `O.nothing`). (b) Conversely, `provenance=[]`/`{}` intended to clear an existing non-empty provenance is indistinguishable from "provenance not supplied"; with unchanged fields/source the guard evaluates `digest == rec.digest and (source is None or source == rec.source) and not provenance` to `True`, so the call returns `O.nothing` and the provenance is silently never cleared. The check should be `(provenance is None or provenance == rec.provenance)`, not `not provenance`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/defs.py (the `O.nothing` guard in `def.updated`)

chunk_findings.detail: The test's name promises two behaviors, but only the whole-definition half is exercised: the only `None` value appears in `def_record` (`{"a": None, "b": 1}` is refused), and every `def_update` call passes a concrete value. An implementation whose `def_update` rejects `None` (e.g. routes updates through the same "null is refused" validation as `def_record`) or stores the literal `None` instead of removing the key passes this test unchanged. The test should have included e.g. `A.def_update(repo, "skill", "s", {"a": None}, agent="a")` and asserted that `a` disappears from `fields`; without it, the stated "null means remove in an update" behavior has zero coverage, while a contradictory implementation still yields `exit == 0` and `{"a": 0, "b": 2}` for the lone update that is performed.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_def_records.py::test_null_means_remove_in_an_update_and_is_refused_in_a_whole_definition

chunk_findings.detail: The test asserts only the merged `provenance` of the provenance-only update, not that `fields` survived the empty `{}` update. Given the recorded `{"b": 1}`, an implementation that treats the empty `fields` argument as "replace fields with the empty set" produces `defs["skill:s"].fields == {}` while still returning `exit == 0` and `provenance == {"by": "a", "reviewed": "yes"}`, so the test passes on a record whose fields were silently wiped. A companion assertion such as `_state(repo).defs["skill:s"].fields == {"b": 1}` would be needed to make this test discriminating.

chunk_findings.detail: `_text` is the only place in the file where a PEP-604 union is evaluated at *runtime*. Every other union in this module (`str | None`, `DD.Answer | None`, `dict | None`, ...) sits inside an annotation and is therefore stringified by the module's `from __future__ import annotations`; the isinstance argument is a normal expression and is evaluated eagerly. On any interpreter older than 3.10 (which is exactly the range that a blanket `from __future__ import annotations` is normally there to support), `str | int | float` raises `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for |: 'type' and 'type'`. Concretely, the most common call into the new path — `def_record(repo, "rule", "r-1", {"text": "x"})`, where `title` and `body` default to `""` — reaches `_text` with `title or body` false and raises instead of returning the `def.recorded` outcome, so recording a definition that has no explicit title/body crashes. The fix is `isinstance(v, (str, int, float))`. If the project's minimum Python is 3.10+, this is a non-issue; but given that the author deliberately deferred every other union, the runtime union here is inconsistent with the rest of the file and is a real failure on the interpreters that pattern implies.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/defs.py `_text` (the `isinstance(v, str | int | float)` line)

chunk_findings.detail:
The back-link from the absorbing record to the merged record is written only if the successor happens to already be in `st.defs` at the moment `def.merged` is folded, and it is never retried. The surrounding fold is explicitly designed to tolerate out-of-order arrival (`_record`'s docstring says a status change or update "created when an update or a status change arrives before its definition (a shard merged out of order)"), but `h_merged` does not honor that: `into = st.defs.get(key(rec.kind, rec.successor))` returns `None`, the `if into is not None` guard swallows it, and `merged_from` is silently lost. Given an event stream (a shard replay where the merge is ordered before the successor's definition) of

1. `def.recorded {kind:"skill", id:"A", fields:{...}}`
2. `def.merged {kind:"skill", id:"A", successor:"B"}`  (B not yet known)
3. `def.recorded {kind:"skill", id:"B", fields:{...}}`

the folded `st.defs["skill:B"].merged_from` ends up `[]` instead of `["A"]`, contradicting the handler's own contract ("Folded into `successor` ... which records that it absorbed this one"). Any consumer that resolves B's provenance from `merged_from` (the very reason the field exists) gets the wrong answer, and unlike a missing `State.defs` entry, the omission is permanent because nothing later re-derives or repairs the link.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/handlers/defs.py `h_merged`

chunk_findings.detail: The test compares `fold(evs).defs` with `fold(list(evs)).defs`, but `list(evs)` is just a copy of `evs`, so both folds receive the identical event sequence in the identical order. The assertion can never fail (for any deterministic fold) and cannot catch order-dependent folding, which is the stated purpose of this area of the fold ("Shards merge out of order: the fold never drops an event for arriving early") and of determinism. A meaningful version would fold a reordered permutation of the same events and assert `.defs` equality.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_def_records.py::test_the_fold_is_deterministic

chunk_findings.detail: The `O.nothing` short-circuit treats `source` idempotently (it compares against `rec.source`) but treats `provenance` as "any non-empty value is a change," never comparing it to `rec.provenance`. So a call that supplies the *same* provenance as already recorded is never recognized as a no-op and emits a fresh `def.updated` event every time. Concretely: a record whose state already holds `provenance = ["p"]` and unchanged fields, called twice as `update(repo, agent, kind, rid, fields={}, source=rec.source, provenance=["p"])`, returns a normal outcome and appends a duplicate `def.updated` event on the second call instead of `O.nothing`. This contradicts the function's contract ("Exit 2 when the result is what is already recorded") and makes provenance-bearing updates non-idempotent / unbounded-event-generating. Either the check should compare `provenance` to `rec.provenance` the way `source` does, or the docstring/contract must be changed to say provenance is an append-only signal.

chunk_findings.detail:
The guard changed from a falsy test to an identity test: old `not provenance` treated both `None` and `{}` as "no provenance supplied"; the new `provenance is None or {...} == rec.provenance` treats `{}` as an explicitly supplied provenance. `{}` is still passed through to `_envelope(cfg, kind, rid, ..., provenance)`, so the write path materialises `{"by": cfg.agent.id}`.

Concrete failure: a record `rec` was created (by agent `A`) with `rec.provenance == {"by": "A", "ticket": "T-1"}`. A caller that normalises its optional argument (`provenance=provenance or {}`) calls `def_update(repo, "A", kind, rid, fields={}, source=None, provenance={})`. Here `digest == rec.digest` and `source is None`, so the old code returned `O.nothing("def.updated", "...nothing changed")`. With the new code `{} is None` is False and `{"by": "A"} != {"by": "A", "ticket": "T-1"}`, so `same_prov` is False and the function falls through: it appends a spurious `def.updated` event and rewrites the stored provenance to `{"by": "A"}`, silently dropping `"ticket"`. If the caller is agent `B` instead, the "nothing changed" call now reassigns provenance to `{"by": "B"}`. The short-circuit that is supposed to make a no-op update idempotent no longer covers the empty-dict case it covered before. Keeping the original falsy semantics (`not provenance or {...} == rec.provenance`) avoids the spurious event and the provenance overwrite.

chunk_findings.detail: `_text` is the only place in the file where a PEP-604 union is evaluated at *runtime*. Every other union in this module (`str | None`, `DD.Answer | None`, `dict | None`, ...) sits inside an annotation and is therefore stringified by the module's `from __future__ import annotations`; the isinstance argument is a normal expression and is evaluated eagerly. On any interpreter older than 3.10 (which is exactly the range that a blanket `from __future__ import annotations` is normally there to support), `str | int | float` raises `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for |: 'type' and 'type'`. Concretely, the most common call into the new path — `def_record(repo, "rule", "r-1", {"text": "x"})`, where `title` and `body` default to `""` — reaches `_text` with `title or body` false and raises instead of returning the `def.recorded` outcome, so recording a definition that has no explicit title/body crashes. The fix is `isinstance(v, (str, int, float))`. If the project's minimum Python is 3.10+, this is a non-issue; but given that the author deliberately deferred every other union, the runtime union here is inconsistent with the rest of the file and is a real failure on the interpreters that pattern implies.

chunk_findings.detail:
The back-link from the absorbing record to the merged record is written only if the successor happens to already be in `st.defs` at the moment `def.merged` is folded, and it is never retried. The surrounding fold is explicitly designed to tolerate out-of-order arrival (`_record`'s docstring says a status change or update "created when an update or a status change arrives before its definition (a shard merged out of order)"), but `h_merged` does not honor that: `into = st.defs.get(key(rec.kind, rec.successor))` returns `None`, the `if into is not None` guard swallows it, and `merged_from` is silently lost. Given an event stream (a shard replay where the merge is ordered before the successor's definition) of

1. `def.recorded {kind:"skill", id:"A", fields:{...}}`
2. `def.merged {kind:"skill", id:"A", successor:"B"}`  (B not yet known)
3. `def.recorded {kind:"skill", id:"B", fields:{...}}`

the folded `st.defs["skill:B"].merged_from` ends up `[]` instead of `["A"]`, contradicting the handler's own contract ("Folded into `successor` ... which records that it absorbed this one"). Any consumer that resolves B's provenance from `merged_from` (the very reason the field exists) gets the wrong answer, and unlike a missing `State.defs` entry, the omission is permanent because nothing later re-derives or repairs the link.

chunk_findings.detail: The test compares `fold(evs).defs` with `fold(list(evs)).defs`, but `list(evs)` is just a copy of `evs`, so both folds receive the identical event sequence in the identical order. The assertion can never fail (for any deterministic fold) and cannot catch order-dependent folding, which is the stated purpose of this area of the fold ("Shards merge out of order: the fold never drops an event for arriving early") and of determinism. A meaningful version would fold a reordered permutation of the same events and assert `.defs` equality.

chunk_findings.detail: The `O.nothing` short-circuit treats `source` idempotently (it compares against `rec.source`) but treats `provenance` as "any non-empty value is a change," never comparing it to `rec.provenance`. So a call that supplies the *same* provenance as already recorded is never recognized as a no-op and emits a fresh `def.updated` event every time. Concretely: a record whose state already holds `provenance = ["p"]` and unchanged fields, called twice as `update(repo, agent, kind, rid, fields={}, source=rec.source, provenance=["p"])`, returns a normal outcome and appends a duplicate `def.updated` event on the second call instead of `O.nothing`. This contradicts the function's contract ("Exit 2 when the result is what is already recorded") and makes provenance-bearing updates non-idempotent / unbounded-event-generating. Either the check should compare `provenance` to `rec.provenance` the way `source` does, or the docstring/contract must be changed to say provenance is an append-only signal.

chunk_findings.detail:
The guard changed from a falsy test to an identity test: old `not provenance` treated both `None` and `{}` as "no provenance supplied"; the new `provenance is None or {...} == rec.provenance` treats `{}` as an explicitly supplied provenance. `{}` is still passed through to `_envelope(cfg, kind, rid, ..., provenance)`, so the write path materialises `{"by": cfg.agent.id}`.

Concrete failure: a record `rec` was created (by agent `A`) with `rec.provenance == {"by": "A", "ticket": "T-1"}`. A caller that normalises its optional argument (`provenance=provenance or {}`) calls `def_update(repo, "A", kind, rid, fields={}, source=None, provenance={})`. Here `digest == rec.digest` and `source is None`, so the old code returned `O.nothing("def.updated", "...nothing changed")`. With the new code `{} is None` is False and `{"by": "A"} != {"by": "A", "ticket": "T-1"}`, so `same_prov` is False and the function falls through: it appends a spurious `def.updated` event and rewrites the stored provenance to `{"by": "A"}`, silently dropping `"ticket"`. If the caller is agent `B` instead, the "nothing changed" call now reassigns provenance to `{"by": "B"}`. The short-circuit that is supposed to make a no-op update idempotent no longer covers the empty-dict case it covered before. Keeping the original falsy semantics (`not provenance or {...} == rec.provenance`) avoids the spurious event and the provenance overwrite.

chunk_findings.detail: `def_record` stores the caller's fields verbatim (`fields=dict(fields)`, `digest = D.digest(fields)`), and `_fields_problem` explicitly accepts JSON `null` (it only rejects non-JSON via `json.dumps(..., allow_nan=False)`). So a definition may legitimately hold a null-valued field. `def_update`, however, filters `None` out of the *combined* dict, not just out of the caller's delta. Given a definition recorded as `def_record(repo, "rule", "r1", {"a": None, "b": 1})`, a later `def_update(repo, "rule", "r1", {"b": 2})` builds `merged = {"b": 2}` and drops `a` entirely, even though the caller never mentioned `a`. The update therefore silently deletes an existing field. The two write paths disagree on what `None` means ("a value" at record time, "remove this key" at update time), and `def_update` also computes its digest from the filtered dict while `def_record` computes it from the unfiltered one, so a record containing any null field will additionally never satisfy the `digest == rec.digest` "nothing changed" check, producing spurious `def.updated` events. Either `def_record` must reject/normalize `None` the same way, or `def_update` must filter only the keys present in `fields`.

chunk_findings.detail: `h_merged` performs a cross-record side effect — appending the merged id to the successor's `merged_from` — by looking the successor up in `st.defs` at the moment the event is folded. This only works if the successor's record already exists. But the module explicitly supports the out-of-order case: `_record` (and its docstring "created when an update or a status change arrives before its definition (a shard merged out of order)") is built precisely so a status change can arrive before the record it targets. `h_merged` is a status change on the *source* record, yet the *successor* is never created/stubbed — it is just fetched. So given the event sequence `def.merged {kind: "rule", id: "A", successor: "B"}` followed by `def.recorded {kind: "rule", id: "B"}`, the fold creates A with status MERGED and successor B, the lookup for B returns `None`, and `B.merged_from` is never populated. The same two events in the opposite order yield `B.merged_from == ["A"]`. The fold is therefore order-dependent and silently loses the "B absorbed A" back-reference in exactly the shard-out-of-order scenario the file claims to handle; unlike `_record`, there is no re-application when B's `def.recorded` later arrives (that handler only resets status/fields and does not re-scan pending merges).

chunk_findings.detail: `assert fold(evs).defs == fold(list(evs)).defs` folds the same list twice (`list(evs)` is a same-order copy), so it is a tautology that cannot fail regardless of whether the fold is order-dependent. The test name claims to verify determinism, but the meaningful property (same result when shard events arrive in a different order) is left unverified, even though the neighboring fold test shows a `def.updated`/`def.recorded` pair is genuinely order-sensitive. Replacing the right-hand side with a reordered copy of the events would make the assertion meaningful.

chunk_findings.detail: The new conjunct `and not provenance` tests truthiness of the supplied provenance instead of comparing it with what is already recorded, so it gets both directions wrong. (a) If a record already has a non-empty provenance `P`, calling `def.updated(repo, agent, kind, rid, fields=<current fields>, source=rec.source, provenance=P)` still falls through the guard (because `not P` is `False`) and emits a fresh `def.updated` event on every call, even though nothing changed: a retry/reconcile loop that re-applies the same update now appends an unbounded stream of no-op events (previously it returned `O.nothing`). (b) Conversely, `provenance=[]`/`{}` intended to clear an existing non-empty provenance is indistinguishable from "provenance not supplied"; with unchanged fields/source the guard evaluates `digest == rec.digest and (source is None or source == rec.source) and not provenance` to `True`, so the call returns `O.nothing` and the provenance is silently never cleared. The check should be `(provenance is None or provenance == rec.provenance)`, not `not provenance`.

chunk_findings.detail: The test's name promises two behaviors, but only the whole-definition half is exercised: the only `None` value appears in `def_record` (`{"a": None, "b": 1}` is refused), and every `def_update` call passes a concrete value. An implementation whose `def_update` rejects `None` (e.g. routes updates through the same "null is refused" validation as `def_record`) or stores the literal `None` instead of removing the key passes this test unchanged. The test should have included e.g. `A.def_update(repo, "skill", "s", {"a": None}, agent="a")` and asserted that `a` disappears from `fields`; without it, the stated "null means remove in an update" behavior has zero coverage, while a contradictory implementation still yields `exit == 0` and `{"a": 0, "b": 2}` for the lone update that is performed.

chunk_findings.detail: When `provenance is None`, `prov` is built as `{k: v for k, v in rec.provenance.items() if k != "by"}`, dropping the recorded author, and `_envelope(cfg, kind, rid, ..., prov)` re-inserts `{"by": cfg.agent.id, ...}`. Concretely: agent A records a def so `rec.provenance == {"by": "A", "src": "imports/x"}`; agent B then calls `update(kind, rid, fields={}, provenance=None)` with no field/source change. `digest == rec.digest` and the source matches, but `same_prov` computes `{"by": "B", "src": "imports/x"} == {"by": "A", "src": "imports/x"}` → `False`, so instead of the intended `O.nothing("def.updated", ... "nothing changed")` the function emits a `def.updated` event carrying `provenance == {"by": "B", "src": "imports/x"}`, and the fold's `_envelope` overwrites `rec.provenance`, silently transferring the recorded writer from A to B. The stated invariant ("Strict fold keeps first writers per kind", and the docstring's own concern that a non-content event "would drop what the content's said") is violated: the first writer's `by` is discarded on any update by another agent, and a no-op write produces an event with an empty `changed` list. Keeping the recorded provenance (`prov = rec.provenance`) would preserve the extra keys the change is trying to protect while leaving the recorded author (and the "nothing changed" result) intact.

chunk_findings.detail:
The test records two definitions with byte-identical fields:

```python
A.def_record(repo, "skill", "s", {"b": 1}, provenance={"via": "import"}, agent="a")
A.def_record(repo, "skill", "t", {"b": 1}, agent="a")
```

Since a definition's digest is computed over its fields alone (cf. the existing context `rec.digest == D.digest({"b": 2})`), `skill:t` has exactly the same digest as `skill:s`. With the uniform add-time duplicate/contradiction check (B-coh-*) that this change is built around, the second `def_record` is a duplicate-content record and is rejected at add time (the same way `("skill", "x", {1: "int key"}, ...)` etc. are rejected in the validation test). The call therefore raises before `def_update`/`def_supersede` ever run, so the test errors out instead of exercising the provenance-persistence behavior it was added for. To test provenance surviving an edit and a status change, the successor `t` must have content distinct from `s` (e.g. `{"b": 3}`); otherwise the duplicate check fires and the test cannot pass.

```python
A.def_record(repo, "skill", "t", {"b": 1}, agent="a")
```

Since a definition's digest is computed over its fields alone (cf. the existing context `rec.digest == D.digest({"b": 2})`), `skill:t` has exactly the same digest as `skill:s`. With the uniform add-time duplicate/contradiction check (B-coh-*) that this change is built around, the second `def_record` is a duplicate-content record and is rejected at add time (the same way `("skill", "x", {1: "int key"}, ...)` etc. are rejected in the validation test). The call therefore raises before `def_update`/`def_supersede` ever run, so the test errors out instead of exercising the provenance-persistence behavior it was added for. To test provenance surviving an edit and a status change, the successor `t` must have content distinct from `s` (e.g. `{"b": 3}`); otherwise the duplicate check fires and the test cannot pass.

chunk_findings.detail: `_text` is the only place in the file where a PEP-604 union is evaluated at *runtime*. Every other union in this module (`str | None`, `DD.Answer | None`, `dict | None`, ...) sits inside an annotation and is therefore stringified by the module's `from __future__ import annotations`; the isinstance argument is a normal expression and is evaluated eagerly. On any interpreter older than 3.10 (which is exactly the range that a blanket `from __future__ import annotations` is normally there to support), `str | int | float` raises `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for |: 'type' and 'type'`. Concretely, the most common call into the new path — `def_record(repo, "rule", "r-1", {"text": "x"})`, where `title` and `body` default to `""` — reaches `_text` with `title or body` false and raises instead of returning the `def.recorded` outcome, so recording a definition that has no explicit title/body crashes. The fix is `isinstance(v, (str, int, float))`. If the project's minimum Python is 3.10+, this is a non-issue; but given that the author deliberately deferred every other union, the runtime union here is inconsistent with the rest of the file and is a real failure on the interpreters that pattern implies.

chunk_findings.detail:
The back-link from the absorbing record to the merged record is written only if the successor happens to already be in `st.defs` at the moment `def.merged` is folded, and it is never retried. The surrounding fold is explicitly designed to tolerate out-of-order arrival (`_record`'s docstring says a status change or update "created when an update or a status change arrives before its definition (a shard merged out of order)"), but `h_merged` does not honor that: `into = st.defs.get(key(rec.kind, rec.successor))` returns `None`, the `if into is not None` guard swallows it, and `merged_from` is silently lost. Given an event stream (a shard replay where the merge is ordered before the successor's definition) of

1. `def.recorded {kind:"skill", id:"A", fields:{...}}`
2. `def.merged {kind:"skill", id:"A", successor:"B"}`  (B not yet known)
3. `def.recorded {kind:"skill", id:"B", fields:{...}}`

the folded `st.defs["skill:B"].merged_from` ends up `[]` instead of `["A"]`, contradicting the handler's own contract ("Folded into `successor` ... which records that it absorbed this one"). Any consumer that resolves B's provenance from `merged_from` (the very reason the field exists) gets the wrong answer, and unlike a missing `State.defs` entry, the omission is permanent because nothing later re-derives or repairs the link.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/handlers/defs.py `h_merged`

chunk_findings.detail: The test compares `fold(evs).defs` with `fold(list(evs)).defs`, but `list(evs)` is just a copy of `evs`, so both folds receive the identical event sequence in the identical order. The assertion can never fail (for any deterministic fold) and cannot catch order-dependent folding, which is the stated purpose of this area of the fold ("Shards merge out of order: the fold never drops an event for arriving early") and of determinism. A meaningful version would fold a reordered permutation of the same events and assert `.defs` equality.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_def_records.py::test_the_fold_is_deterministic

chunk_findings.detail: The `O.nothing` short-circuit treats `source` idempotently (it compares against `rec.source`) but treats `provenance` as "any non-empty value is a change," never comparing it to `rec.provenance`. So a call that supplies the *same* provenance as already recorded is never recognized as a no-op and emits a fresh `def.updated` event every time. Concretely: a record whose state already holds `provenance = ["p"]` and unchanged fields, called twice as `update(repo, agent, kind, rid, fields={}, source=rec.source, provenance=["p"])`, returns a normal outcome and appends a duplicate `def.updated` event on the second call instead of `O.nothing`. This contradicts the function's contract ("Exit 2 when the result is what is already recorded") and makes provenance-bearing updates non-idempotent / unbounded-event-generating. Either the check should compare `provenance` to `rec.provenance` the way `source` does, or the docstring/contract must be changed to say provenance is an append-only signal.

chunk_findings.detail:
The guard changed from a falsy test to an identity test: old `not provenance` treated both `None` and `{}` as "no provenance supplied"; the new `provenance is None or {...} == rec.provenance` treats `{}` as an explicitly supplied provenance. `{}` is still passed through to `_envelope(cfg, kind, rid, ..., provenance)`, so the write path materialises `{"by": cfg.agent.id}`.

Concrete failure: a record `rec` was created (by agent `A`) with `rec.provenance == {"by": "A", "ticket": "T-1"}`. A caller that normalises its optional argument (`provenance=provenance or {}`) calls `def_update(repo, "A", kind, rid, fields={}, source=None, provenance={})`. Here `digest == rec.digest` and `source is None`, so the old code returned `O.nothing("def.updated", "...nothing changed")`. With the new code `{} is None` is False and `{"by": "A"} != {"by": "A", "ticket": "T-1"}`, so `same_prov` is False and the function falls through: it appends a spurious `def.updated` event and rewrites the stored provenance to `{"by": "A"}`, silently dropping `"ticket"`. If the caller is agent `B` instead, the "nothing changed" call now reassigns provenance to `{"by": "B"}`. The short-circuit that is supposed to make a no-op update idempotent no longer covers the empty-dict case it covered before. Keeping the original falsy semantics (`not provenance or {...} == rec.provenance`) avoids the spurious event and the provenance overwrite.

chunk_findings.detail: `grant` builds the `approval.granted` payload and adds `token_hash` **only** when `single_use=True` (`if token: data["token_hash"] = token_hash(token)`), and it never writes `used_at` at all — the `Approval.token` comment even states the hash is kept in the log for a minted token, with `""` for a standing approval. `check` then indexes those two keys unconditionally on every row it matched: `standing = [r for r in same if not r["token_hash"]]` and `if r["used_at"]:`. Given the shape this file itself writes, a standing approval (exactly what `ddflow approve reviewer:critic <digest>` produces for the migrated D-reviewer-trust flow) makes the first lookup raise `KeyError: 'token_hash'` instead of returning `Verdict(True, f"{subject} approved by {standing[-1]['user']}")`, and a freshly granted single-use approval makes the second raise `KeyError: 'used_at'` on the first presentation of its token, so neither the standing path nor the single-use path can return a verdict. The two keys are only safe if the (unseen) `State.approvals` projection backfills `token_hash: ""` / `used_at: None` for the events this writer emits; if the projection keeps the granted payload as appended — which is what `Verdict.row`'s "as `State.approvals` keeps it" and `grant`'s "recorded only as its hash" suggest — the failure is `KeyError` at the very first approval check.

chunk_findings.detail: The change declares (in the intent) the primitive as `Approval(subject, digest, actor, token)`, i.e. `actor` and `token` are sibling fields on the approval record (`token` is the separate uniqueness/nonce field, `actor` is the approving identity). The code then treats the actor field as a *container* by reading `granted.actor.user`. If `actor` is the identity value itself — a string such as the OS user the old `_user()` produced and that the old event stored under `"user"` — then `granted.actor.user` raises `AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'user'`. The demonstration is the ordinary path: `approve(repo, "my-model")` reaches `AP.grant(...)`, the approval is recorded, and the very next line `who = granted.actor.user` throws before the function can return the "reviewer ... approved by ..." message, so every reviewer approval crashes even though the grant succeeded. The correct read would be `who = granted.actor` (with the old `"user"` value now living in the `actor` field), or the call should name a `Granted`/`Actor` wrapper explicitly if one exists — the diff does neither, and nothing else in the changed lines supplies a structured actor.

chunk_findings.detail: `h_granted` populates `st.reviewer_approvals` for *any* `approval.granted` whose resolved subject starts with `reviewer:`, without consulting the event's `human` flag. The legacy writer of that table (`gates._h_reviewer_approved`) explicitly hardcodes `{"human": True}` precisely because a reviewer approval is person-only, and the entries it writes into `reviewer_approvals` carry no `human` field at all — so the reviewer-trust checks that read this table (as the module docstring states) have no way to distinguish a person from an agent. The new path therefore creates a non-human writer where none existed. Concretely, an `approval.granted` event with data `{"subject": "reviewer:evil", "digest": "<cfg-digest>", "human": false}` is folded at line 44-51 into `st.reviewer_approvals["<cfg-digest>"] = {"name": "evil", ...}`, giving `evil` the same trusted-reviewer status a human approval would, which contradicts the stated intent that the reviewer approval surface stays "person-only as today" and that `approval.granted` records "the digest *a person* approved" (`human` recorded but never enforced on this branch).

chunk_findings.detail: `grant` writes `token_hash` only when `single_use=True` and never writes `used_at`, yet `check`/`use` index both keys directly. Given the existing reviewer flow, `grant(log, "reviewer:critic", d)` (default `single_use=False`) appends `approval.granted` with `data = {"subject": ..., "digest": ..., "user": ..., "host": ..., "human": true, "note": ...}` — no `token_hash`. A subsequent `check(state, "reviewer:critic", d)` evaluates `not r["token_hash"]` on that row and raises `KeyError: 'token_hash'` instead of returning the `Verdict(True, ...)` the standing approval is supposed to produce; the same happens at `if r["used_at"]` for any single-use approval whose grant row was never mutated to carry `used_at`. This is the first flow moved onto the primitive (D-reviewer-trust, a standing approval), so it fails on its primary path unless the fold happens to synthesize `token_hash`/`used_at` keys the grant event never contained — an obligation this file's own writer does not meet, and which the `approval.used` payload (`{"subject", "digest", "token_hash"}`, no `used_at`) likewise does not meet for the spent marker.

chunk_findings.detail:
`approve()` previously recorded the approval event with the bare reviewer name as its subject:

```python
_log(Path(repo), "").append("reviewer.approved", name, {...})
```

The new code records it under a namespaced subject:

```python
granted = AP.grant(
    _log(Path(repo), ""),
    "reviewer:" + name,   # <-- was `name`
    dig,
    ...
)
```

The reader function immediately above this hunk still looks approvals up by the bare name:

```python
return (snapshot(repo) or {}).get(name, ("", ""))[0]
```

`snapshot(repo)` is the structure that answers "what digest has this reviewer approved?" (it is what `_approved_digest`/`pending` rely on: `pending()` is documented as "Reviewers whose CURRENT entry a tool wrote and no person has approved"). If `snapshot` keys its entries by the approval event's subject — which is exactly what the old `name`-keyed `.get(name, ...)` implies — then after this change an operator who runs `ddflow approve <reviewer>` writes a `"reviewer:<name>"` entry that `.get(name, ...)` will never find. Concretely: approve reviewer `alice`, then call `approved_digest(repo, "alice", st)`; it returns `("", "")[0]`, i.e. the empty digest, and `alice` remains reported as unapproved. Because re-approving writes the same namespaced subject, the reviewer can never reach an approved state, and any check that compares the running digest against the approved one will fail (or, if written as `if approved and approved != digest`, silently skip the comparison). Either the new subject namespace must be applied to the lookup (e.g. `"reviewer:" + name`) or the approval primitive's own reader must be used on this side; as written the persisted key and the read key disagree.

chunk_findings.detail: `grant` builds the `approval.granted` payload and adds `token_hash` **only** when `single_use=True` (`if token: data["token_hash"] = token_hash(token)`), and it never writes `used_at` at all — the `Approval.token` comment even states the hash is kept in the log for a minted token, with `""` for a standing approval. `check` then indexes those two keys unconditionally on every row it matched: `standing = [r for r in same if not r["token_hash"]]` and `if r["used_at"]:`. Given the shape this file itself writes, a standing approval (exactly what `ddflow approve reviewer:critic <digest>` produces for the migrated D-reviewer-trust flow) makes the first lookup raise `KeyError: 'token_hash'` instead of returning `Verdict(True, f"{subject} approved by {standing[-1]['user']}")`, and a freshly granted single-use approval makes the second raise `KeyError: 'used_at'` on the first presentation of its token, so neither the standing path nor the single-use path can return a verdict. The two keys are only safe if the (unseen) `State.approvals` projection backfills `token_hash: ""` / `used_at: None` for the events this writer emits; if the projection keeps the granted payload as appended — which is what `Verdict.row`'s "as `State.approvals` keeps it" and `grant`'s "recorded only as its hash" suggest — the failure is `KeyError` at the very first approval check.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approval.py — `grant` vs `check` (row keys `token_hash`, `used_at`)

chunk_findings.detail: The change declares (in the intent) the primitive as `Approval(subject, digest, actor, token)`, i.e. `actor` and `token` are sibling fields on the approval record (`token` is the separate uniqueness/nonce field, `actor` is the approving identity). The code then treats the actor field as a *container* by reading `granted.actor.user`. If `actor` is the identity value itself — a string such as the OS user the old `_user()` produced and that the old event stored under `"user"` — then `granted.actor.user` raises `AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'user'`. The demonstration is the ordinary path: `approve(repo, "my-model")` reaches `AP.grant(...)`, the approval is recorded, and the very next line `who = granted.actor.user` throws before the function can return the "reviewer ... approved by ..." message, so every reviewer approval crashes even though the grant succeeded. The correct read would be `who = granted.actor` (with the old `"user"` value now living in the `actor` field), or the call should name a `Granted`/`Actor` wrapper explicitly if one exists — the diff does neither, and nothing else in the changed lines supplies a structured actor.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reviewer_trust.py `who = granted.actor.user`

chunk_findings.detail: The fold handler and the new check disagree about whether a row may lack the `human` key. `AP.check` now reads `[r for r in state.approvals.get(subject, []) if r.get("human")]`, and its own comment states that "a hand-written grant that does not say `human` is none" — i.e. the check is written to tolerate a row in which `human` is absent and treat it as not-a-person's-approval. But the fold handler that populates `state.approvals` indexes the key directly: `if subject.startswith(REVIEWER) and row["human"]`. Given a hand-written `approval.granted` event for a reviewer subject that omits the key, e.g. `Event(kind="approval.granted", subject="reviewer:x", data={"subject": "reviewer:x", "digest": "abc"}, ...)`, folding raises `KeyError: 'human'` at that line before `check` is ever reached — so the input that `check` was specifically written to reject crashes replay instead, and `verdict.ok` never returns False. The new test only exercises `human: False` (key present), so the omitted-key case the comment describes is untested and unhandled. Either the handler should use `row.get("human")` like the check, or the check's `.get`/comment is misleading about the accepted schema.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/handlers/approvals.py:44

chunk_findings.detail: `h_granted` populates `st.reviewer_approvals` for *any* `approval.granted` whose resolved subject starts with `reviewer:`, without consulting the event's `human` flag. The legacy writer of that table (`gates._h_reviewer_approved`) explicitly hardcodes `{"human": True}` precisely because a reviewer approval is person-only, and the entries it writes into `reviewer_approvals` carry no `human` field at all — so the reviewer-trust checks that read this table (as the module docstring states) have no way to distinguish a person from an agent. The new path therefore creates a non-human writer where none existed. Concretely, an `approval.granted` event with data `{"subject": "reviewer:evil", "digest": "<cfg-digest>", "human": false}` is folded at line 44-51 into `st.reviewer_approvals["<cfg-digest>"] = {"name": "evil", ...}`, giving `evil` the same trusted-reviewer status a human approval would, which contradicts the stated intent that the reviewer approval surface stays "person-only as today" and that `approval.granted` records "the digest *a person* approved" (`human` recorded but never enforced on this branch).

chunk_findings.detail: `grant` writes `token_hash` only when `single_use=True` and never writes `used_at`, yet `check`/`use` index both keys directly. Given the existing reviewer flow, `grant(log, "reviewer:critic", d)` (default `single_use=False`) appends `approval.granted` with `data = {"subject": ..., "digest": ..., "user": ..., "host": ..., "human": true, "note": ...}` — no `token_hash`. A subsequent `check(state, "reviewer:critic", d)` evaluates `not r["token_hash"]` on that row and raises `KeyError: 'token_hash'` instead of returning the `Verdict(True, ...)` the standing approval is supposed to produce; the same happens at `if r["used_at"]` for any single-use approval whose grant row was never mutated to carry `used_at`. This is the first flow moved onto the primitive (D-reviewer-trust, a standing approval), so it fails on its primary path unless the fold happens to synthesize `token_hash`/`used_at` keys the grant event never contained — an obligation this file's own writer does not meet, and which the `approval.used` payload (`{"subject", "digest", "token_hash"}`, no `used_at`) likewise does not meet for the spent marker.

chunk_findings.detail:
`approve()` previously recorded the approval event with the bare reviewer name as its subject:

```python
_log(Path(repo), "").append("reviewer.approved", name, {...})
```

The new code records it under a namespaced subject:

```python
granted = AP.grant(
    _log(Path(repo), ""),
    "reviewer:" + name,   # <-- was `name`
    dig,
    ...
)
```

The reader function immediately above this hunk still looks approvals up by the bare name:

```python
return (snapshot(repo) or {}).get(name, ("", ""))[0]
```

`snapshot(repo)` is the structure that answers "what digest has this reviewer approved?" (it is what `_approved_digest`/`pending` rely on: `pending()` is documented as "Reviewers whose CURRENT entry a tool wrote and no person has approved"). If `snapshot` keys its entries by the approval event's subject — which is exactly what the old `name`-keyed `.get(name, ...)` implies — then after this change an operator who runs `ddflow approve <reviewer>` writes a `"reviewer:<name>"` entry that `.get(name, ...)` will never find. Concretely: approve reviewer `alice`, then call `approved_digest(repo, "alice", st)`; it returns `("", "")[0]`, i.e. the empty digest, and `alice` remains reported as unapproved. Because re-approving writes the same namespaced subject, the reviewer can never reach an approved state, and any check that compares the running digest against the approved one will fail (or, if written as `if approved and approved != digest`, silently skip the comparison). Either the new subject namespace must be applied to the lookup (e.g. `"reviewer:" + name`) or the approval primitive's own reader must be used on this side; as written the persisted key and the read key disagree.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reviewer_trust.py:185 (approve → AP.grant call)

chunk_findings.detail: The new `check` filter deliberately treats a grant that "does not say `human`" as non-human by using `r.get("human")`, but the fold path uses direct subscripting `row["human"]`. Rows in `state.approvals` come from the same event data that `check` reads, so a hand-written `approval.granted` whose `data` omits the `human` key and whose subject starts with `reviewer:` — exactly the grant this change is supposed to neutralize — makes `row["human"]` raise `KeyError` during fold instead of being silently ignored. Reproduction: take `test_a_grant_that_is_not_a_persons_approves_nothing` and drop `"human": False` from the event `data` (i.e. `data={"subject": "reviewer:evil", "digest": "abc"}`); `fold([ev])` now raises `KeyError: 'human'` rather than returning a state in which `check` reports not-approved. Since `check` goes out of its way to accept an absent `human`, the two paths disagree about the same input, and a single such appended event aborts state folding for every subsequent command. The fix is to use `row.get("human")` in fold as well.

chunk_findings.detail: The new single-range diff drops unreviewed item commits whenever the item committed after the last review and *then* merged `base`. Concretely: suppose the branch has commit `H` that was just reviewed (so `head = H`), the agent then commits an item change `B`, and then runs `git merge main`, producing merge commit `X` with parents `B` and `mainTip`. Now `ddflow review <id> --delta` calls `_delta_start(repo, tip, head, base)`, which (per its own docstring, "against `head` merged with `base`'s incoming work") returns the merge commit `X`. The tip path then runs `git diff X <tip>` (the `start != head` branch), and `X`'s tree already contains `B`, so `B` is not in the output at all — an unreviewed commit is silently omitted and the reviewer approves code it never saw (severity HIGH: wrong review, not just wasted capacity). The same happens in the worktree path, where `committed = W.git(wt, "diff", start, "HEAD")` is likewise taken from `X`. Conversely, if `_delta_start` were to return `head` in this situation, the range `head..HEAD` still contains `mainTip`'s incoming commits, i.e. the original Bccf6d1aec7 leak (560-695k chars of other items' code) is unfixed. Only the special case where `head` is a direct parent of the merge works; any delta that must both keep item commits made before the merge and exclude commits reachable from `main` cannot be produced by a single `git diff start tip` and needs e.g. a range over `head..HEAD --not <base>` (or per-commit diffs) rather than one start commit.

chunk_findings.detail:
`merge-base --all <base> <tip>` returns **two** OIDs whenever base and tip have a criss‑cross relationship, and with more than one base `_delta_start` unconditionally returns `head`. The callers then fall back to `git diff head...tip` (worktree path: `capture_diff(wt, head)`), which — because `head` is an ancestor of `tip` in this situation — is exactly `head..tip`, i.e. every commit `tip` gained since the review, *including everything that came in from main*. That is precisely the behavior bug Bccf6d1aec7 asks to remove.

Concrete repro: main is at `M0`; item branch commits `B1` and it is reviewed (head = `B1`). Main advances to `M1`, and the branch does `git merge main` → `tip = MB` (parents `B1`, `M1`). Meanwhile main merges the branch's older tip `B1` → `main = MM` (parents `M1`, `B1`). Now `merge-base --all main tip` = `{M1, B1}` (neither is an ancestor of the other), so `len(bases) == 2`, `_delta_start` returns `head = B1`, and `ddflow review --delta` emits `diff B1..MB`, which contains all of `M1`'s (main's) changes. The reviewer again receives another item's already‑reviewed code.

This is arguably a regression versus the code being replaced: the old singular `merge-base base tip` only returned `head` when there was *no* usable base or when that base was already an ancestor of `head`; on a criss‑cross it would still attempt `merge-tree`. The new code guarantees the fallback. (The regression test described — plain `git merge main` with unrelated changes, no mutual merge — has exactly one merge base and therefore never exercises this path, so it passes while the bug persists.)

chunk_findings.detail: Switching from `git merge-base` to `git merge-base --all` and bailing to `head` whenever more than one merge base exists re-sends exactly the un-fixed range the bug is about. When `_delta_start` returns `head`, the callers degrade to `git diff head...tip` / `git diff head...<branch>`, i.e. the full reviewed-head-to-tip range, which contains every commit that came in from `main`. Concrete input: item branch B forks main at F, then B merges main at M (branch has a merge commit whose second parent is M), and main has separately merged B's tip T (main has a merge commit whose second parent is T); now `git merge-base --all main B` prints both M and T, so `_delta_start` returns `head` and `ddflow review <id> --delta` once again ships all of main's incoming commits to the reviewer — the exact Bccf6d1aec7 symptom the change claims to fix. The README's justification ("as before") is not accurate: the old `merge-base` (without `--all`) selected a single best base and still produced a merged tree, so the delta stayed bounded; this change makes the multi-base case strictly worse. The guard is only justified if you accept reintroducing the bug for those histories.

chunk_findings.detail: The baseline is built favouring `head` on conflicts, so any conflicting hunk that main changed and the item resolved toward main is absent from the baseline but present in HEAD, and `git diff start <tip>` emits main's already-reviewed code as if it were the item's change. Concrete input: at the reviewed head, file f contains `"H"` (the item's version); the base had `"base"` and main's merged commit has `"M"`; the item's merge commit resolves f to `"M"` (accepting main's side). `_delta_start` returns the tree of `merge-tree(head, came_in, -X ours)`, whose f is `"H"`, so the caller emits a `-"H" +"M"` hunk — main's content is sent to the reviewer, refutable-by-hand findings about another agent's change. The stated fix is to "exclude commits reachable from main"; only favouring the incoming side (`-X theirs`) puts main's conflicting version into the baseline and drops that hunk. `-X ours` excludes main's non-conflicting commits but deliberately re-admits its conflicting ones, which is the same class of waste the bug reports.

chunk_findings.detail:
`merge-base --all <base> <tip>` returns **two** OIDs whenever base and tip have a criss‑cross relationship, and with more than one base `_delta_start` unconditionally returns `head`. chunk_findings.detail: The new single-range diff drops unreviewed item commits whenever the item committed after the last review and *then* merged `base`. Concretely: suppose the branch has commit `H` that was just reviewed (so `head = H`), the agent then commits an item change `B`, and then runs `git merge main`, producing merge commit `X` with parents `B` and `mainTip`. Now `ddflow review <id> --delta` calls `_delta_start(repo, tip, head, base)`, which (per its own docstring, "against `head` merged with `base`'s incoming work") returns the merge commit `X`. The tip path then runs `git diff X <tip>` (the `start != head` branch), and `X`'s tree already contains `B`, so `B` is not in the output at all — an unreviewed commit is silently omitted and the reviewer approves code it never saw (severity HIGH: wrong review, not just wasted capacity). The same happens in the worktree path, where `committed = W.git(wt, "diff", start, "HEAD")` is likewise taken from `X`. Conversely, if `_delta_start` were to return `head` in this situation, the range `head..HEAD` still contains `mainTip`'s incoming commits, i.e. the original Bccf6d1aec7 leak (560-695k chars of other items' code) is unfixed. Only the special case where `head` is a direct parent of the merge works; any delta that must both keep item commits made before the merge and exclude commits reachable from `main` cannot be produced by a single `git diff start tip` and needs e.g. a range over `head..HEAD --not <base>` (or per-commit diffs) rather than one start commit.

chunk_findings.detail: `test_a_conflicted_merge_still_sends_none_of_mains_other_work` never resolves the conflict it creates. The merge at line 99 conflicts on `shared.py` (both `item` and `main` modify `v = 0`), and line 100 rewrites the working-tree copy to `v = 'resolved'`, but the file is never staged (`git add shared.py` is missing). `_git` runs with `check=True`, and `git commit -a` refuses to commit while the index still holds the unmerged stage-1/2/3 entries, dying with `error: Committing is not possible because you have unmerged files.` / `fatal: Exiting because of an unresolved conflict.` Consequently line 101 raises `CalledProcessError` and the test errors out before either assertion is reached — on the fixed and unfixed code alike. The scenario the docstring describes therefore never exercises `_delta_diff` with a merge-resolution commit, so the regression coverage this test is supposed to provide for the conflict case does not exist.

chunk_findings.detail:
`merge-base --all <base> <tip>` returns **two** OIDs whenever base and tip have a criss‑cross relationship, and with more than one base `_delta_start` unconditionally returns `head`. The callers then fall back to `git diff head...tip` (worktree path: `capture_diff(wt, head)`), which — because `head` is an ancestor of `tip` in this situation — is exactly `head..tip`, i.e. every commit `tip` gained since the review, *including everything that came in from main*. That is precisely the behavior bug Bccf6d1aec7 asks to remove.

Concrete repro: main is at `M0`; item branch commits `B1` and it is reviewed (head = `B1`). Main advances to `M1`, and the branch does `git merge main` → `tip = MB` (parents `B1`, `M1`). Meanwhile main merges the branch's older tip `B1` → `main = MM` (parents `M1`, `B1`). Now `merge-base --all main tip` = `{M1, B1}` (neither is an ancestor of the other), so `len(bases) == 2`, `_delta_start` returns `head = B1`, and `ddflow review --delta` emits `diff B1..MB`, which contains all of `M1`'s (main's) changes. The reviewer again receives another item's already‑reviewed code.

This is arguably a regression versus the code being replaced: the old singular `merge-base base tip` only returned `head` when there was *no* usable base or when that base was already an ancestor of `head`; on a criss‑cross it would still attempt `merge-tree`. The new code guarantees the fallback. (The regression test described — plain `git merge main` with unrelated changes, no mutual merge — has exactly one merge base and therefore never exercises this path, so it passes while the bug persists.)

chunk_findings.detail: The change flips the conflict resolution of the synthetic merge from `-X ours` to `-X theirs`. In `git merge-tree --write-tree <start> <commit>`, the *first* argument is "ours" and the *second* is "theirs"; here `start` is `head` (the item) and `commit` is the incoming merge-base commit from `main`. `-X theirs` therefore makes the synthetic tree contain **main's** version of every conflicted hunk, and the delta is then `git diff <that tree> tip`. Concretely: item reviewed at `head` with `f = "item"`; main has `f = "main"`; the item merges main and resolves the conflict by keeping its own side, so `tip` has `f = "item"`. The synthetic merge now resolves to `f = "main"`, so the delta emitted is `-main +item` — the reviewer is sent the incoming `main` (another item's) code, plus the item's already-reviewed line, instead of nothing. The pre-change code resolved to `head`'s side and produced an empty delta for this (common) case. This is precisely the class of leak the change claims to eliminate ("exclude commits reachable from main", "only the item's own new changes are sent"), and it can be arbitrarily large when the conflicted file is large. The rewritten docstring ("where the two conflict the incoming side is kept") documents the flipped behavior but does not make it correct with respect to the stated goal; the old docstring's rationale for keeping head's side (so the diff shows how the item resolved the conflict without re-sending the base's content) still applies.

chunk_findings.detail: The merge is launched with `capture_output=True` but its result object is discarded, and nothing asserts that the merge actually conflicted (or even ran). The whole regression value of this test depends on `main`'s commits — in particular the `theirs.py` commit — being pulled into the item's history. If `git merge` does not bring them in, `theirs.py` is never reachable from the item's HEAD, so the final assertion `"theirs.py" not in diff and "+x = 1" in diff` holds *even on the unfixed code*, and the test silently stops guarding bug Bccf6d1aec7. Concretely, with `git config --global merge.ff only` (or `merge.ff` set to `only`/`false` in a CI image), `git merge main` aborts with "Not possible to fast-forward, aborting" because `item` has diverged; the item worktree never receives `theirs.py`, yet `_git(tree, "rm", "-q", "gone.py")` still resolves, the commit and `own.py` commit succeed, and the test passes with the bug still present. The same happens if `main` is not the repository's branch name (e.g. a fixture using `init.defaultBranch=master`): `git merge main` fails, the test still goes green. The test should assert the merge's expected conflict (e.g. `assert result.returncode != 0` / that the tree contains a conflicted `gone.py`), or assert `theirs.py` is reachable in `tree` before resolving the conflict, so a non-merging run cannot masquerade as a passing regression test.

chunk_findings.detail:
The conflict-resolution side was flipped from `-X ours` to `-X theirs`, which re-introduces main's incoming code into the very delta the fix is supposed to purify.

Concrete failure: item branch head `H` has `foo:10 = X` (already reviewed). `main` (tip `M2`) has `foo:10 = Y`. `git merge main` conflicts and the author resolves it by keeping the item's side, so the merge commit `T` has `foo:10 = X`. Delta review runs with `base = main = M2`, `tip = T`, `head = H`:

- `merge-base --all M2 T` → `[M2]`, and `M2` is not an ancestor of `H` → `came_in = [M2]`.
- `merge-tree --write-tree -X theirs H M2` keeps the *incoming* side at the conflict, so the base tree has `foo:10 = Y`.
- `_delta_diff` then returns `git diff <base-tree> T` = `-Y / +X`.

The reviewer receives main's incoming line `Y` (other items' code, "already reviewed elsewhere") even though the item made no change at all since the last reviewed head — the item merely kept its own version, so the correct delta is empty. This is exactly bug Bccf6d1aec7's symptom reappearing for any merge that had conflicts, and the rewritten docstring ("shows exactly where the item's result departs from the base's") does not save it: departing from *main's* side is not the item's own new work, it is main's work that the item declined.

The `-X ours` form used before was correct for this contract: the base tree is `head` plus main's non-conflicting merge, so `git diff base T` yields only the item's resolution and its post-merge commits. With `-X ours` the "kept my side" case yields an empty diff (right), and the "adopted main's side" case yields `X→Y` (the item's real change); with `-X theirs` the first case fabricates a diff out of main's lines and the second case hides the item's change entirely. Note the regression test as described ("merge main with unrelated changes") uses a conflict-free merge, so it cannot catch this.

chunk_findings.detail: The new single-range diff drops unreviewed item commits whenever the item committed after the last review and *then* merged `base`. Concretely: suppose the branch has commit `H` that was just reviewed (so `head = H`), the agent then commits an item change `B`, and then runs `git merge main`, producing merge commit `X` with parents `B` and `mainTip`. Now `ddflow review <id> --delta` calls `_delta_start(repo, tip, head, base)`, which (per its own docstring, "against `head` merged with `base`'s incoming work") returns the merge commit `X`. The tip path then runs `git diff X <tip>` (the `start != head` branch), and `X`'s tree already contains `B`, so `B` is not in the output at all — an unreviewed commit is silently omitted and the reviewer approves code it never saw (severity HIGH: wrong review, not just wasted capacity). The same happens in the worktree path, where `committed = W.git(wt, "diff", start, "HEAD")` is likewise taken from `X`. Conversely, if `_delta_start` were to return `head` in this situation, the range `head..HEAD` still contains `mainTip`'s incoming commits, i.e. the original Bccf6d1aec7 leak (560-695k chars of other items' code) is unfixed. Only the special case where `head` is a direct parent of the merge works; any delta that must both keep item commits made before the merge and exclude commits reachable from `main` cannot be produced by a single `git diff start tip` and needs e.g. a range over `head..HEAD --not <base>` (or per-commit diffs) rather than one start commit.
