chunk_findings.detail: `test_a_conflicted_merge_still_sends_none_of_mains_other_work` never resolves the conflict it creates. The merge at line 99 conflicts on `shared.py` (both `item` and `main` modify `v = 0`), and line 100 rewrites the working-tree copy to `v = 'resolved'`, but the file is never staged (`git add shared.py` is missing). `_git` runs with `check=True`, and `git commit -a` refuses to commit while the index still holds the unmerged stage-1/2/3 entries, dying with `error: Committing is not possible because you have unmerged files.` / `fatal: Exiting because of an unresolved conflict.` Consequently line 101 raises `CalledProcessError` and the test errors out before either assertion is reached — on the fixed and unfixed code alike. The scenario the docstring describes therefore never exercises `_delta_diff` with a merge-resolution commit, so the regression coverage this test is supposed to provide for the conflict case does not exist.

chunk_findings.detail:
`merge-base --all <base> <tip>` returns **two** OIDs whenever base and tip have a criss‑cross relationship, and with more than one base `_delta_start` unconditionally returns `head`. The callers then fall back to `git diff head...tip` (worktree path: `capture_diff(wt, head)`), which — because `head` is an ancestor of `tip` in this situation — is exactly `head..tip`, i.e. every commit `tip` gained since the review, *including everything that came in from main*. That is precisely the behavior bug Bccf6d1aec7 asks to remove.

Concrete repro: main is at `M0`; item branch commits `B1` and it is reviewed (head = `B1`). Main advances to `M1`, and the branch does `git merge main` → `tip = MB` (parents `B1`, `M1`). Meanwhile main merges the branch's older tip `B1` → `main = MM` (parents `M1`, `B1`). Now `merge-base --all main tip` = `{M1, B1}` (neither is an ancestor of the other), so `len(bases) == 2`, `_delta_start` returns `head = B1`, and `ddflow review --delta` emits `diff B1..MB`, which contains all of `M1`'s (main's) changes. The reviewer again receives another item's already‑reviewed code.

This is arguably a regression versus the code being replaced: the old singular `merge-base base tip` only returned `head` when there was *no* usable base or when that base was already an ancestor of `head`; on a criss‑cross it would still attempt `merge-tree`. The new code guarantees the fallback. (The regression test described — plain `git merge main` with unrelated changes, no mutual merge — has exactly one merge base and therefore never exercises this path, so it passes while the bug persists.)

chunk_findings.detail: The change flips the conflict resolution of the synthetic merge from `-X ours` to `-X theirs`. In `git merge-tree --write-tree <start> <commit>`, the *first* argument is "ours" and the *second* is "theirs"; here `start` is `head` (the item) and `commit` is the incoming merge-base commit from `main`. `-X theirs` therefore makes the synthetic tree contain **main's** version of every conflicted hunk, and the delta is then `git diff <that tree> tip`. Concretely: item reviewed at `head` with `f = "item"`; main has `f = "main"`; the item merges main and resolves the conflict by keeping its own side, so `tip` has `f = "item"`. The synthetic merge now resolves to `f = "main"`, so the delta emitted is `-main +item` — the reviewer is sent the incoming `main` (another item's) code, plus the item's already-reviewed line, instead of nothing. The pre-change code resolved to `head`'s side and produced an empty delta for this (common) case. This is precisely the class of leak the change claims to eliminate ("exclude commits reachable from main", "only the item's own new changes are sent"), and it can be arbitrarily large when the conflicted file is large. The rewritten docstring ("where the two conflict the incoming side is kept") documents the flipped behavior but does not make it correct with respect to the stated goal; the old docstring's rationale for keeping head's side (so the diff shows how the item resolved the conflict without re-sending the base's content) still applies.

chunk_findings.detail: The failure fallback was changed from `return came_in[-1]` to `return head`. `head` is the reviewed head, so the caller's delta becomes `head..tip`, which is the full range since the last review — including every commit that arrived from main. That is precisely bug Bccf6d1aec7: the incoming, already-reviewed code is sent to the reviewer again. Concretely: another item deletes (or renames) file `F`, the item branch also modified `F` and merged main; `git merge-tree --write-tree -X theirs head main_tip` cannot resolve a modify/delete conflict (this conflict type is not resolved by `-X theirs`), so the command exits non-zero, `merged.ok` is false, `tree` is `""`, and the function returns `head`. The delta is then `head..tip` and carries all of main's incoming commits — the 560–695k-character flood the change was supposed to remove. The old code returned the incoming merge base here, whose diff to the tip excludes main's commits entirely, so this change makes the failure path strictly worse with respect to the stated goal. The updated docstring/README assertion that this is "as before this fix" is also false: the immediately preceding code returned `came_in[-1]`, not `head`, so this path did not previously leak main's incoming commits. The proposed regression test ("merge main with unrelated changes") uses a merge that succeeds, so it never exercises this fallback and will not catch the regression.

chunk_findings.detail: The merge is launched with `capture_output=True` but its result object is discarded, and nothing asserts that the merge actually conflicted (or even ran). The whole regression value of this test depends on `main`'s commits — in particular the `theirs.py` commit — being pulled into the item's history. If `git merge` does not bring them in, `theirs.py` is never reachable from the item's HEAD, so the final assertion `"theirs.py" not in diff and "+x = 1" in diff` holds *even on the unfixed code*, and the test silently stops guarding bug Bccf6d1aec7. Concretely, with `git config --global merge.ff only` (or `merge.ff` set to `only`/`false` in a CI image), `git merge main` aborts with "Not possible to fast-forward, aborting" because `item` has diverged; the item worktree never receives `theirs.py`, yet `_git(tree, "rm", "-q", "gone.py")` still resolves, the commit and `own.py` commit succeed, and the test passes with the bug still present. The same happens if `main` is not the repository's branch name (e.g. a fixture using `init.defaultBranch=master`): `git merge main` fails, the test still goes green. The test should assert the merge's expected conflict (e.g. `assert result.returncode != 0` / that the tree contains a conflicted `gone.py`), or assert `theirs.py` is reachable in `tree` before resolving the conflict, so a non-merging run cannot masquerade as a passing regression test.

chunk_findings.detail: When the branch has merged `base` since `head`, `start` is the merge point (different from `head`) and the delta is taken as `git diff --no-color start tip`. If that single call is not `ok`, `if d is None or not d.ok:` falls through to `git diff --no-color f"{head}...{tip}"`. After a merge of `base` into the branch, `head` is an ancestor of `tip` (it is a parent of the merge commit), so `merge-base(head, tip) == head` and `head...tip` is exactly `head..tip` — the range that contains every commit that came in from `base`. So on any failure of the merge-aware diff the function silently emits the other items' code, which is the precise payload bug Bccf6d1aec7 exists to suppress, and it contradicts the function's own docstring ("Raises RuntimeError when no diff can be produced"). This is reachable whenever `_delta_start` yields a value git cannot resolve (its failure return is typically `""`, and `git diff "" tip` errors while `git diff head...tip` succeeds), e.g. a repo where the default branch ref doesn't resolve. The worktree path (`_delta_of_tree`) deliberately raises in the analogous "could not run" case, so the two paths behave inconsistently: one refuses to guess, the other guesses in the direction of sending unreviewed main commits.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review.py:_delta_of_branch

chunk_findings.detail: On the branch path (`item.worktree` unusable, only the branch name is available), when the primary "merged-baseline" diff fails, `_delta_diff` falls back to `git diff <head>...<branch>`, which is precisely the pre-fix range. The test proves which command is allowed to succeed: the monkeypatch fails every diff whose argv does not contain `f"{head}...item"`, and the assertion `assert "+x = 2" in diff` only passes because that `head...branch` diff is produced. But after `git merge main`, `head...branch` (== `head..branch`, since the reviewed head is an ancestor of HEAD) contains every commit the merge pulled in — in the test's own `merged` fixture that includes `theirs.py` with its 200 lines of main's work. The test never asserts `"theirs.py" not in diff` here, so it green-lights a fallback that re-sends main's incoming work. This is not hypothetical: the worktree path has to cope with an unresolvable synthetic merge (the modify/delete conflict modelled by `test_a_merge_that_cannot_be_written_still_sends_none_of_mains_work`) and it survives by falling back to main's tip, which is safe; the branch path has the same failure mode but falls back to the whole range instead, i.e. to exactly the 560-695k characters of other items' code this change exists to remove. Any such failure on a post-merge branch silently produces an inflated delta over main's commits rather than refusing, contradicting the stated "refused with the reason, not reported as 'nothing changed'" policy.

chunk_findings.detail:
The reworked test cannot fail on the unfixed code, so it does not guard the behavior the fix introduces. The stub now makes *every* `git diff` fail:

```python
lambda where, *a, **k: RV.W.GitResult(1, "", "boom") if a[:1] == ("diff",) else real(where, *a, **k)
```

On the pre-change `_delta_diff` in `ddflow/api/review.py`, a `start != head` call does `git diff start tip` (fails, `err="boom"`), then unconditionally falls back to `git diff {head}...{tip}` (also fails, `err="boom"`), and finally raises `RuntimeError("git diff ... failed: boom")` — which satisfies `pytest.raises(RuntimeError, match="boom")`. The same holds when `start == head` (the only diff is the `head...tip` fallback). So running this test against the unmodified `review.py` passes it, exactly as it passes with the fix; it never observes whether the wider `head...tip` range was retried. (The old stub was already discriminating but was removed instead of retargeted.)

A discriminating version would keep the selective stub — fail only diffs that are not the `{head}...item` range, i.e. `if a[:1] == ("diff",) and f"{head}...item" not in a:` — and then assert `with pytest.raises(RuntimeError, match="simulated failure")`. On the unfixed code the fallback `git diff {head}...item` would succeed and return `+x = 2`, so no exception would be raised and the test would fail; on the fixed code the refusal is raised and the test passes.

Now `ddflow review <id> --delta` calls `_delta_start(repo, tip, head, base)`, which (per its own docstring, "against `head` merged with `base`'s incoming work") returns the merge commit `X`. chunk_findings.detail:
`merge-base --all <base> <tip>` returns **two** OIDs whenever base and tip have a criss‑cross relationship, and with more than one base `_delta_start` unconditionally returns `head`. The callers then fall back to `git diff head...tip` (worktree path: `capture_diff(wt, head)`), which — because `head` is an ancestor of `tip` in this situation — is exactly `head..tip`, i.e. every commit `tip` gained since the review, *including everything that came in from main*. That is precisely the behavior bug Bccf6d1aec7 asks to remove.

Concrete repro: main is at `M0`; item branch commits `B1` and it is reviewed (head = `B1`). Main advances to `M1`, and the branch does `git merge main` → `tip = MB` (parents `B1`, `M1`). Meanwhile main merges the branch's older tip `B1` → `main = MM` (parents `M1`, `B1`). Now `merge-base --all main tip` = `{M1, B1}` (neither is an ancestor of the other), so `len(bases) == 2`, `_delta_start` returns `head = B1`, and `ddflow review --delta` emits `diff B1..MB`, which contains all of `M1`'s (main's) changes. The new code guarantees the fallback. (The regression test described — plain `git merge main` with unrelated changes, no mutual merge — has exactly one merge base and therefore never exercises this path, so it passes while the bug persists.)

chunk_findings.detail: When the branch has merged `base` since `head`, `start` is the merge point (different from `head`) and the delta is taken as `git diff --no-color start tip`. If that single call is not `ok`, `if d is None or not d.ok:` falls through to `git diff --no-color f"{head}...{tip}"`. After a merge of `base` into the branch, `head` is an ancestor of `tip` (it is a parent of the merge commit), so `merge-base(head, tip) == head` and `head...tip` is exactly `head..tip` — the range that contains every commit that came in from `base`. So on any failure of the merge-aware diff the function silently emits the other items' code, which is the precise payload bug Bccf6d1aec7 exists to suppress, and it contradicts the function's own docstring ("Raises RuntimeError when no diff can be produced"). This is reachable whenever `_delta_start` yields a value git cannot resolve (its failure return is typically `""`, and `git diff "" tip` errors while `git diff head...tip` succeeds), e.g. a repo where the default branch ref doesn't resolve. The worktree path (`_delta_of_tree`) deliberately raises in the analogous "could not run" case, so the two paths behave inconsistently: one refuses to guess, the other guesses in the direction of sending unreviewed main commits.

chunk_findings.detail: On the branch path (`item.worktree` unusable, only the branch name is available), when the primary "merged-baseline" diff fails, `_delta_diff` falls back to `git diff <head>...<branch>`, which is precisely the pre-fix range. The test proves which command is allowed to succeed: the monkeypatch fails every diff whose argv does not contain `f"{head}...item"`, and the assertion `assert "+x = 2" in diff` only passes because that `head...branch` diff is produced. But after `git merge main`, `head...branch` (== `head..branch`, since the reviewed head is an ancestor of HEAD) contains every commit the merge pulled in — in the test's own `merged` fixture that includes `theirs.py` with its 200 lines of main's work. The test never asserts `"theirs.py" not in diff` here, so it green-lights a fallback that re-sends main's incoming work. This is not hypothetical: the worktree path has to cope with an unresolvable synthetic merge (the modify/delete conflict modelled by `test_a_merge_that_cannot_be_written_still_sends_none_of_mains_work`) and it survives by falling back to main's tip, which is safe; the branch path has the same failure mode but falls back to the whole range instead, i.e. to exactly the 560-695k characters of other items' code this change exists to remove. chunk_findings.detail:
The reworked test cannot fail on the unfixed code, so it does not guard the behavior the fix introduces. The stub now makes *every* `git diff` fail:

```python
lambda where, *a, **k: RV.W.GitResult(1, "", "boom") if a[:1] == ("diff",) else real(where, *a, **k)
```

On the pre-change `_delta_diff` in `ddflow/api/review.py`, a `start != head` call does `git diff start tip` (fails, `err="boom"`), then unconditionally falls back to `git diff {head}...{tip}` (also fails, `err="boom"`), and finally raises `RuntimeError("git diff ... failed: boom")` — which satisfies `pytest.raises(RuntimeError, match="boom")`. The same holds when `start == head` (the only diff is the `head...tip` fallback). So running this test against the unmodified `review.py` passes it, exactly as it passes with the fix; it never observes whether the wider `head...tip` range was retried. (The old stub was already discriminating but was removed instead of retargeted.)

A discriminating version would keep the selective stub — fail only diffs that are not the `{head}...item` range, i.e. `if a[:1] == ("diff",) and f"{head}...item" not in a:` — and then assert `with pytest.raises(RuntimeError, match="simulated failure")`. On the unfixed code the fallback `git diff {head}...item` would succeed and return `+x = 2`, so no exception would be raised and the test would fail; on the fixed code the refusal is raised and the test passes.

chunk_findings.detail: The pre‑existing line `older = ev.data.get(OLDER_MARK)` was changed to read the marker from the *upcast* event `cur` instead of the event as it was logged (`ev`). `OLDER_MARK` is provenance metadata describing which ddflow version wrote the record, not part of the payload shape that upcasters target; the upcaster contract stated in this change is only "returning the current shape". Concretely: take a real log from a released version containing `{"kind": "session.prompt", "data": {"v": 1, "<OLDER_MARK>": "1.4", ...}}`, and an upcaster registered for `("session.prompt", 1)` that normalizes the payload to the current shape (e.g. builds the new dict from the fields the current schema declares, or renames a field the ratchet required an upcaster for). `upcast` returns that normalized event, `cur.data.get(OLDER_MARK)` is `None`, and `if older:` is false — so `st.older_version_events` silently stops incrementing for old‑version events, and the compat report/doctor output states the log contains no older‑version events even though every event in it came from 1.4. Because the original code read `ev.data`, the marker was counted correctly before this change; the new read location is what drops it. Reading the marker must happen on the raw event (before/independently of `upcast`), where it is defined.

chunk_findings.detail: The new non-strict error isolation only wraps `upcast(ev)` and `handler(st, cur)`. The line `older = cur.data.get(OLDER_MARK)` sits between them, outside every `try`, so an event whose `data` is not a dict still aborts the entire fold — in both strict and non-strict mode — which is exactly the failure the change claims to fix ("One malformed event no longer aborts the fold ... and the fold continues"). The same diff adds `isinstance(ev.data, dict)` to the `adopted` comprehension, showing the author already knows `Event.data` can be a non-dict (e.g. a log line whose payload was `null` or a JSON array). Concrete input: an event of kind `item.created` with `data = []`. `upcast` returns the version-1 object unchanged, so control reaches `cur.data.get(OLDER_MARK)`, which raises `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'`. That exception is not caught by the `except Exception` around `upcast` (already passed) nor by the handler `try` (not yet entered), so `fold(events, strict=False)` propagates instead of appending a `FoldProblem` and continuing. The guard for non-dict payloads needs to cover this read too (or the `older`/handler dispatch must move inside the protected block).

chunk_findings.detail: The change replaces the explicit defensive copy `dict(data or {})` with `UP.stamp(kind, data or {})`, and `stamp` is documented by the accompanying comment as a no-op for version-1 kinds ("absent at version 1, so the bytes written are unchanged") — i.e. it hands the caller's own dict through rather than a copy. Everything after that line mutates `payload` in place: the append path attaches the log's provenance `OLDER_MARK` (the model.py comment states "Provenance the LOG added to the payload"), and, when `self.stamp` is set, the version/skew stamp. With the copy gone, those keys land in the object the caller still owns. Demonstrated by `d = {"n": 1}; log.append("k", d)`: `d` is now `{"n": 1, OLDER_MARK: ..., <version>: ...}` after the call, whereas before the change it stayed `{"n": 1}`. A caller that reuses the same dict for a second append, hashes/compares it, or passes it to another kind's append now silently carries stale provenance/version that the previous `dict(...)` copy prevented.

chunk_findings.detail: The new "is the removal named in the contract" check is a raw substring test: `if f"`{kind}` v{was['v'] + 1}" not in contract` (and the identical `... or f"`{k}` v{snap[k]['v'] + 1}" not in contract` in the ratchet). Because the version token is not delimited, any *higher* version entry for the same kind satisfies a lower-version requirement. Concrete input: a kind `k.a` whose snapshot version is 1, an upcaster registered from v1 (`steps={"k.a": [1]}`), and a contract that contains only `` `k.a` v20 becomes k.b ``. Then `` `k.a` v2 `` is a substring of `` `k.a` v20 becomes k.b ``, so `drift(old, {"format": 1, "kinds": {}}, steps={"k.a": [1]}, contract="`k.a` v20 becomes k.b")` returns `[]` instead of the expected `k.a: removal (v2) is not named ...` message, and the ratchet test's `gone` also omits `k.a`. The result is that a breaking removal which the contract never names at the required version is silently accepted — exactly the failure the ratchet exists to prevent. The check needs an exact token match (e.g., a regex with a non-digit boundary after the version) rather than `in`.

The change's stated rule is "A removed kind, a removed field or a changed type fails the test unless an upcaster is registered and the contract doc names the change", and for removed fields / retyped fields the function does enforce the contract (via the version-bump path). For a removed kind it does not: the sibling test `test_the_snapshot_records_every_kind_at_its_current_version` likewise only demands an upcaster, and `test_every_version_bump_has_its_upcasters_and_a_contract_entry` iterates `U.PAYLOAD_VERSIONS`, which contains no entry for a kind that was deleted. Concretely, the test file itself demonstrates the hole: `drift(old, {"format": 1, "kinds": {}}, steps={"k.a": [1]}, contract="")` is asserted to return `[]`. So a branch that deletes a kind and registers `("k.a", 1)` in `upcasters.UPCASTERS` but forgets to document the removal in `compatibility.md` passes the ratchet, which is exactly the case the intent says must fail. (The `drift` signature already accepts `contract`, so the fix is a contract lookup in this branch, plus a contract assertion in `test_the_snapshot_records_every_kind_at_its_current_version`.)

data.summary: Event.from_json accepts {"data": [1,2]} (or null, a string, a number). The resulting Event reaches readers that take data as a mapping -- the fold (aborting even a non-strict one), doctor's _orphan_notes, stamp_facts -- and each raises AttributeError, so one hand-edited or corrupt line breaks doctor and every read. Found by roborev (kilo) on B-uni-compat-events. Fix: from_json refuses a non-object data, so the log reader counts the line as unreadable (which doctor already reports).

chunk_findings.detail: The pre‑existing line `older = ev.data.get(OLDER_MARK)` was changed to read the marker from the *upcast* event `cur` instead of the event as it was logged (`ev`). `OLDER_MARK` is provenance metadata describing which ddflow version wrote the record, not part of the payload shape that upcasters target; the upcaster contract stated in this change is only "returning the current shape". Concretely: take a real log from a released version containing `{"kind": "session.prompt", "data": {"v": 1, "<OLDER_MARK>": "1.4", ...}}`, and an upcaster registered for `("session.prompt", 1)` that normalizes the payload to the current shape (e.g. builds the new dict from the fields the current schema declares, or renames a field the ratchet required an upcaster for). `upcast` returns that normalized event, `cur.data.get(OLDER_MARK)` is `None`, and `if older:` is false — so `st.older_version_events` silently stops incrementing for old‑version events, and the compat report/doctor output states the log contains no older‑version events even though every event in it came from 1.4. Because the original code read `ev.data`, the marker was counted correctly before this change; the new read location is what drops it. Reading the marker must happen on the raw event (before/independently of `upcast`), where it is defined.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/model.py:371 (`older = cur.data.get(OLDER_MARK)`)

chunk_findings.detail: The change replaces the explicit defensive copy `dict(data or {})` with `UP.stamp(kind, data or {})`, and `stamp` is documented by the accompanying comment as a no-op for version-1 kinds ("absent at version 1, so the bytes written are unchanged") — i.e. it hands the caller's own dict through rather than a copy. Everything after that line mutates `payload` in place: the append path attaches the log's provenance `OLDER_MARK` (the model.py comment states "Provenance the LOG added to the payload"), and, when `self.stamp` is set, the version/skew stamp. With the copy gone, those keys land in the object the caller still owns. Demonstrated by `d = {"n": 1}; log.append("k", d)`: `d` is now `{"n": 1, OLDER_MARK: ..., <version>: ...}` after the call, whereas before the change it stayed `{"n": 1}`. A caller that reuses the same dict for a second append, hashes/compares it, or passes it to another kind's append now silently carries stale provenance/version that the previous `dict(...)` copy prevented.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log.py:860 (`payload = UP.stamp(kind, data or {})`)

chunk_findings.detail: The new "is the removal named in the contract" check is a raw substring test: `if f"`{kind}` v{was['v'] + 1}" not in contract` (and the identical `... or f"`{k}` v{snap[k]['v'] + 1}" not in contract` in the ratchet). Because the version token is not delimited, any *higher* version entry for the same kind satisfies a lower-version requirement. Concrete input: a kind `k.a` whose snapshot version is 1, an upcaster registered from v1 (`steps={"k.a": [1]}`), and a contract that contains only `` `k.a` v20 becomes k.b ``. Then `` `k.a` v2 `` is a substring of `` `k.a` v20 becomes k.b ``, so `drift(old, {"format": 1, "kinds": {}}, steps={"k.a": [1]}, contract="`k.a` v20 becomes k.b")` returns `[]` instead of the expected `k.a: removal (v2) is not named ...` message, and the ratchet test's `gone` also omits `k.a`. The result is that a breaking removal which the contract never names at the required version is silently accepted — exactly the failure the ratchet exists to prevent. The check needs an exact token match (e.g., a regex with a non-digit boundary after the version) rather than `in`.

chunk_findings.detail: The new non-strict error isolation only wraps `upcast(ev)` and `handler(st, cur)`. The line `older = cur.data.get(OLDER_MARK)` sits between them, outside every `try`, so an event whose `data` is not a dict still aborts the entire fold — in both strict and non-strict mode — which is exactly the failure the change claims to fix ("One malformed event no longer aborts the fold ... and the fold continues"). The same diff adds `isinstance(ev.data, dict)` to the `adopted` comprehension, showing the author already knows `Event.data` can be a non-dict (e.g. a log line whose payload was `null` or a JSON array). Concrete input: an event of kind `item.created` with `data = []`. `upcast` returns the version-1 object unchanged, so control reaches `cur.data.get(OLDER_MARK)`, which raises `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'`. That exception is not caught by the `except Exception` around `upcast` (already passed) nor by the handler `try` (not yet entered), so `fold(events, strict=False)` propagates instead of appending a `FoldProblem` and continuing. The guard for non-dict payloads needs to cover this read too (or the `older`/handler dispatch must move inside the protected block).

chunk_findings.detail: The new payload guard only validates `data`, but computes it with `d.get("data", {})` before checking that `d` itself is a mapping. For any log line that is valid JSON but not a JSON object — a hand-edited/corrupted shard line like `[1, 2]`, `"x"`, `42`, or `null` — `json.loads` returns a list/str/int/None and `d.get(...)` raises `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'`. Before this change the same line failed one line later at `d["kind"]`, i.e. with `TypeError`. The author chose `TypeError` for the new guard precisely because that is the exception the log reader is expected to catch ("The log reader counts the line as unreadable"); under that same assumption the top-level non-object case now escapes with `AttributeError`, which is not the type the reader handles, so a single such line can still abort the read (and doctor/fold) — the exact outcome the comment claims to prevent. If the reader is in fact catching the wrong-but-universal `Exception`, the change is harmless, but as written the guard is inconsistent: it silently relies on the reader catching `TypeError` while introducing an `AttributeError` for the neighbouring malformed-line class. Checking `isinstance(d, dict)` before `.get` (or wrapping the `.get` in the same `TypeError`) would keep every non-object line in the one bucket the reader already handles.

The stated defect is in the changed-path listing (`W.git` invoked without `-z` and with renames enabled, so a rename's old path is dropped and non-ASCII names come back C-quoted), but the only production change here is a behavior-preserving refactor: the `NOT_LISTED` sentinel is replaced by a `listed: bool = True` keyword, and the call site becomes `_scope_fields(outside, listed=borrowed)`. chunk_findings.detail: `_record_merge_gate` returns early (records nothing) whenever the `merge` gate is human, and the failed branch throws that return value away. So for a project that declares the merge gate human, a real, attempted, failed `git merge` no longer produces any `merge`/`failed` outcome at all. The comment two lines above this call explicitly documents why that outcome matters: “A merge that was tried and failed is a merge-gate outcome: the log-derived `merge_failure_rate` flow signal counts it, and without this it saw successes only.” A human checkpoint concerns whether the *gate* is cleared by a person; it has nothing to do with whether the underlying git operation failed. Demonstrated input: `.ddflow/gates.toml` marks `merge` as a human gate, then run `ddflow merge` on a branch with a conflicting upstream; the merge is attempted and fails, `r.attempted` is true, but `_record_merge_gate` sees `gdef.is_human_gate` and returns `True` without calling `G.record`, so no `failed` outcome is written and `merge_failure_rate` silently under-counts failures exactly for the projects that opted into the human gate. (The `passed` path legitimately wants to suppress recording for a human gate; the failure path does not.)
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/merge.py:122 (`if r.attempted:` branch → `_record_merge_gate(..., "failed", ...)`)

chunk_findings.detail: `_record_merge_gate` returns early — *before* `G.record` is ever called — whenever the project's `merge` gate is human, for **every** outcome, not just `"passed"`. At the failed-merge call site the boolean is discarded and execution proceeds, so a merge that was tried and failed on a human-gated project writes nothing to the log. That directly reintroduces the condition the comment immediately above the call site (unchanged, ~lines 117–119) says this record exists to prevent: "A merge that was tried and failed is a merge-gate outcome: the log-derived `merge_failure_rate` flow signal counts it, and without this it saw successes only." Concretely: put `.ddflow/gates.toml` with `merge` declared as a human checkpoint, run a merge whose preconditions pass but whose git attempt fails (`r.attempted` is true, `r.err/r.out` set); previously (and per the comment) a `"failed"` `merge` outcome is appended, now `gdef.is_human_gate` is true so the helper returns `True` and `merge_failure_rate` sees only successes for that project. A failed attempt does not clear a human gate, so it should not be routed through the human-gate suppression; the guard belongs only on the `"passed"` path.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new call is placed on the normal return path of `merge`, immediately after the `kept_reason` print and *before* any check that the landing actually happened, so it also fires for merges that failed. On a human-gate project (`[gate.merge] human = true`), take the exact setup of the new `test_a_failed_merge_writes_no_agent_outcome_on_a_human_merge_gate`: `a.py` is changed and committed on the base branch so the landing conflicts, then `run_cli(repo, "merge", "T1")` returns non-zero. `out.data` still carries `merge_gate_human`, so the operator is told:

    the merge gate is a human checkpoint: it is not recorded by merge -- ask the operator to run `ddflow approve T1 merge`

But no merge landed and no gate was reached, so instructing the operator to approve `T1 merge` (and asserting "it is not recorded by merge", a statement that is only meaningful once the merge exists) is wrong; if `approve` does not itself re-check that a landing occurred, this can pass the human checkpoint for a merge that never happened. The accompanying test only asserts `code != 0` and the absence of a recorded outcome on this path — it never asserts the message is absent — which is why the mis-emitted instruction is not caught. The announcement should be emitted only on the landing path (e.g. gated on the merge/`sha` being present), not on the conflict path.

chunk_findings.detail: `_record_merge_gate` returns early (records nothing) whenever the `merge` gate is human, and the failed branch throws that return value away. So for a project that declares the merge gate human, a real, attempted, failed `git merge` no longer produces any `merge`/`failed` outcome at all. The comment two lines above this call explicitly documents why that outcome matters: “A merge that was tried and failed is a merge-gate outcome: the log-derived `merge_failure_rate` flow signal counts it, and without this it saw successes only.” A human checkpoint concerns whether the *gate* is cleared by a person; it has nothing to do with whether the underlying git operation failed. Demonstrated input: `.ddflow/gates.toml` marks `merge` as a human gate, then run `ddflow merge` on a branch with a conflicting upstream; the merge is attempted and fails, `r.attempted` is true, but `_record_merge_gate` sees `gdef.is_human_gate` and returns `True` without calling `G.record`, so no `failed` outcome is written and `merge_failure_rate` silently under-counts failures exactly for the projects that opted into the human gate. (The `passed` path legitimately wants to suppress recording for a human gate; the failure path does not.)

chunk_findings.detail: The stated bug is that the merge path calls `outcomes.record(...)` without `gates=`, so `outcomes.record` skips the human-gate guard (B279a0ebfc1), and the stated fix is "one measured record path (B-uni-gate-record)" that routes through `api/gates.record` with the order check and tree measurement. The delivered diff contains **no functional change at all** — the only production edit is re-wording the docstring of `_record_merge_gate` (lines 205–208). No call site gains `gates=`, no call is redirected through `gates.record`, and the guard in `outcomes.record` is therefore still bypassed exactly as before. Whatever behavior the new docstring promises ("passed OR failed" suppressed for a human checkpoint, `merge_failure_rate` becoming `None`), nothing in this diff arranges for it. A reviewer can confirm mechanically: `git diff` over the change touches only comments and test asserts. The bug cannot be considered fixed by this change.

chunk_findings.detail:
The added assertion
```python
assert "ddflow approve" not in out + err  # nothing landed: no approval to ask for
```
sits in the pre-existing merge-**conflict** test: a conflicting commit is made on main, `merge T1` fails (`code != 0`), and the surrounding assertions already require `_merge_outcomes(repo) == []` and no recorded `gate_outcome`. That path never reaches gate recording — it aborts on the conflict before any outcome is written — so this assertion is true regardless of whether `gates=` is passed to `outcomes.record`. It therefore cannot fail on the unfixed code, which is the explicit acceptance criterion for this bug ("The fix starts with a regression test that fails on the current code"). A test that exercises the guard must drive a *successful* (landed) merge whose `merge` gate is a human checkpoint and assert that no outcome is recorded; the conflict scenario shown does not do that and provides false confidence that the guard is enforced.

chunk_findings.detail: `_record_merge_gate` returns early — *before* `G.record` is ever called — whenever the project's `merge` gate is human, for **every** outcome, not just `"passed"`. At the failed-merge call site the boolean is discarded and execution proceeds, so a merge that was tried and failed on a human-gated project writes nothing to the log. That directly reintroduces the condition the comment immediately above the call site (unchanged, ~lines 117–119) says this record exists to prevent: "A merge that was tried and failed is a merge-gate outcome: the log-derived `merge_failure_rate` flow signal counts it, and without this it saw successes only." Concretely: put `.ddflow/gates.toml` with `merge` declared as a human checkpoint, run a merge whose preconditions pass but whose git attempt fails (`r.attempted` is true, `r.err/r.out` set); previously (and per the comment) a `"failed"` `merge` outcome is appended, now `gdef.is_human_gate` is true so the helper returns `True` and `merge_failure_rate` sees only successes for that project. A failed attempt does not clear a human gate, so it should not be routed through the human-gate suppression; the guard belongs only on the `"passed"` path.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new call is placed on the normal return path of `merge`, immediately after the `kept_reason` print and *before* any check that the landing actually happened, so it also fires for merges that failed. On a human-gate project (`[gate.merge] human = true`), take the exact setup of the new `test_a_failed_merge_writes_no_agent_outcome_on_a_human_merge_gate`: `a.py` is changed and committed on the base branch so the landing conflicts, then `run_cli(repo, "merge", "T1")` returns non-zero. `out.data` still carries `merge_gate_human`, so the operator is told:

    the merge gate is a human checkpoint: it is not recorded by merge -- ask the operator to run `ddflow approve T1 merge`

But no merge landed and no gate was reached, so instructing the operator to approve `T1 merge` (and asserting "it is not recorded by merge", a statement that is only meaningful once the merge exists) is wrong; if `approve` does not itself re-check that a landing occurred, this can pass the human checkpoint for a merge that never happened. The accompanying test only asserts `code != 0` and the absence of a recorded outcome on this path — it never asserts the message is absent — which is why the mis-emitted instruction is not caught. The announcement should be emitted only on the landing path (e.g. gated on the merge/`sha` being present), not on the conflict path.

chunk_findings.detail:
The diff contains no functional change: it edits one docstring and adds one assertion. The bug report (B279a0ebfc1) identifies concrete call sites that "record without passing gates=": `api/lifecycle/merge.py:123`, `api/review.py:1019`, `api/review.py:1156`, and `services/flow.py:385`. None of those lines are touched here. The only `merge.py` hunk is the docstring/`gates = G.load_gates(...)` preamble around line 203; the actual `outcomes.record(...)` invocation(s) are unchanged, so if the guard was skipped because `gates=` was not passed, it is still skipped. Demonstrating input: a project whose `merge` gate is a HUMAN checkpoint, followed by a successful (or failed) merge — `_record_merge_gate` still reaches whatever record call exists below line 213 with no `gates=` argument, so `outcomes.record` runs without the human-gate guard and produces an outcome, exactly what the new docstring and the intent claim no longer happens. The docstring now asserts behavior ("gets no outcome from this command, passed OR failed") that this change does not establish.

The added test line does not close the gap either: `assert "ddflow approve" not in out + err` (tests/test_merge_gate_guard.py:54) inspects human-readable CLI text, not the gate-recording path, and the surrounding outcome assertions (`_merge_outcomes(repo) == []`, `gate_outcome("merge")` is falsy) are pre-existing context lines, not additions. This covers only the conflict-failure path already asserted before; it cannot detect a record call that omits `gates=` on the merge/review/flow paths named in the bug. So the "regression test that fails on the current code" the intent requires is absent, and the claimed fix is not present in the diff.

evidence.note: Checked: proc_start/alive no longer raise on a non-UTF-8 comm (real child renamed via /proc/self/comm); a comm containing ')' still parses (rsplit on the last ')'); a reused pid with a different start time is dead; an older registration without pid_start still counts (pinned); woken/deadline-only and other-host waits never consult the pid (unchanged); jobs.status's own reuse check unaffected. proc_start and alive now share jobs._stat (one lenient /proc reader in services). harness_identity._stat (infra) is a second lenient parser of the same file; infra cannot import services, and the one infra procinfo is B-uni-proc (which needs this fix) -- left to it, noted for its author.

chunk_findings.detail: The change removes **two** deferred import statements — `from .jobs import alive, proc_start` inside `waits._pid_alive` and `from .jobs import proc_start` inside the wait-registration function — and replaces them with a single module-level `from .jobs import alive, proc_start` in `ddflow/services/waits.py`. Only module-level imports are counted by the deferred-imports guard, so the number of tracked deferred sites drops from 618 to **616**, yet the baseline in this file is lowered by only one, to 617. The file's own rule is that the baseline must be lowered "in the same change that removes sites", and its failure message "prints the exact value", i.e. the guard compares the computed count against the baseline and reports a mismatch. With this diff the guard computes 616 against a baseline of 617 and fails (`deferred imports: 616, baseline 617`). chunk_findings.detail: The diff contains no fix at all — it only relocates `alive`/`proc_start` from deferred to module-scope imports. The code the intent identifies as broken is untouched: `jobs.proc_start` (jobs.py:59) and `jobs.alive` (jobs.py:103) still call `read_text()` on `/proc/<pid>/stat`. For a process whose `comm` field holds non-UTF-8 bytes (e.g. `prctl(PR_SET_NAME, b"\xff\xfe")`, or an exec with an invalid-UTF-8 argv[0] that libc copies into comm), `read_text()` raises `UnicodeDecodeError` before any parsing. `waits._pid_alive` still calls `alive(pid)` and `register` still calls `proc_start(w.pid)`, and nothing in the changed code converts or catches that error (a `UnicodeDecodeError` is not an `OSError`), so registering or liveness-checking such a pid still crashes exactly as reported. Likewise the pid-reuse/start-time behavior of `_pid_alive` is unchanged. The intended fix (bytes + lenient decode, new procinfo infra) and the required failing-first regression test are both absent, so the change does not resolve B7395b84149.

chunk_findings.detail: `register` writes the kernel start time into the in-memory object (waits.py:146-147, `w.pid_start = proc_start(w.pid)`), but the wait's persisted representation is the explicit field mapping whose closing brace is the line immediately preceding `_pid_alive` (new line 114) — the same kind of explicit field list that had to be extended in `_validate` (new line 287, `... w.host, w.pid_start`) and the only such list in this diff that was *not* extended. If that mapping is the field-by-field dict it appears to be (the class also carries a `Path`, so serialization cannot simply be `asdict`), then a registered wait record never contains `pid_start`. On the next process that loads the file, `pid_start` defaults to `""`, `_pid_alive(self.pid, "")` short-circuits to a bare `alive(self.pid)`, and the reuse check added at lines 117-124 never runs. Concrete sequence: process A calls `waits.register(w)` and exits; the kernel hands A's pid to a new process B; a third process loads the wait file written by A and calls `live()`; `alive(pid)` sees B and returns True, `started` is `""` so no start-time comparison happens, and the dead wait is reported live — the exact B7395b84149 symptom this change claims to fix. In other words, the fix only works for a `Wait` that never crosses the file boundary, which is precisely the case the bug report is about.

data.title: core/clock now_iso, parse_ts, epoch and age_s with a table test pinning every old parser; the parsers and writers move; a ratchet keeps fromisoformat/strptime in core/clock
fmt_minute, fmt_date and fmt_age replace the repeated [:16]/[:10] slicing and age formatting

data.body:
Found by the unification survey (2026-10-06). Parsers: core/progress.py:81 (strptime, then fromisoformat; 0.0 on failure), api/reporting/records._epoch (fromisoformat; 0.0), services/sessions._age_s (microseconds only; inf otherwise, bug filed), compaction.py:114, triggers.py:246 and export/query.py:200 (naive treated as UTC; None vs raise), quota.py:118 (raises on naive), kind_bugs.py:43 and kind_worklog.py:87 (date only). Writers: core/events.utcnow (microseconds) vs quota._now (seconds, different Z handling). Before migrating, a table test pins every helper's result over these shapes: with and without microseconds, Z, +00:00, naive, date only, garbage. Any change in a result is filed as a bug first. A guard ratchet then allows fromisoformat/strptime only in core/clock. quota keeps its seconds precision through a parameter.

Survey 2026-10-06: Also the display formatting: [:16].replace('T',' ') is repeated 7 times (viewers_sessions.py:30, kind_sessions.py:83/91/101/102, markdown.py:301, knowledge.py:620, export.py:103), [:10] about 8 times although registry.date() exists, and age/minute formatting appears in enforce.py:1027, brief.py:20, commands/lifecycle.py:174, cli.py:151/168/176 and operations.py:83. 'Now' strings are built in rules.py:33, viewers.py:89, gates/runner.py:67 and reservations.py:180. Add fmt_minute(ts), fmt_date(ts) and fmt_age(seconds). The failure sentinels differ (0.0, inf, None): keep the caller's meaning explicit.

Unification survey 2026-10-06: Also: parse_duration('30m'), with _s aliases for the trigger knobs that are in minutes today (triggers.py:70-75 window, debounce and cooldown; every other knob is _s; quota's own k/m/g parser at quota.py:44/127). The MCP caps waits at 1800 s (tools/_common.py:36) but the CLI wait (wait.py:263) has no cap: one limit for both. run_stamp(at=None) for run and file ids (api/review.py:531 uses local time plus uuid4[:8]; jobs:119 time_ns; waits:144 token_hex; flowstate:146 pid plus time_ns). Make ids._free public as ids.free, replacing triggers.py:443-447 and importer._unique:829.

Split into: B-uni-clock.1-parse, B-uni-clock.2-format, B-uni-clock.3-duration, B-uni-clock.4-stamps.

chunk_findings.detail: `parse_date` is documented as accepting ``YYYY-MM-DD`` *exactly* and raising `ValueError` otherwise, but it delegates straight to `date.fromisoformat`. Since this module already requires Python 3.11+ (it does `from datetime import UTC`, which only exists on 3.11+), `date.fromisoformat` is the extended parser: `parse_date("20240101")` returns `datetime.date(2024, 1, 1)` and `parse_date("2024-W01-1")` returns the corresponding week date, instead of raising as the contract states. A caller that uses `parse_date` to validate a date field (the docstring even tells callers to feed it the first ten characters of a timestamp) will therefore silently accept basic-format and week-date strings that are not the extended `YYYY-MM-DD` form the docstring promises to enforce, rather than rejecting them.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/clock.py `parse_date`

chunk_findings.detail: Both call sites were moved onto the new `clock` parsers but kept `except ValueError`, while the sibling call site in `ddflow/services/compaction.py:114` was explicitly rewritten to `except clock.UNPARSEABLE`. A clock API that raises `clock.UNPARSEABLE` and is caught as such in one place but as `ValueError` in two others can only be correct if `UNPARSEABLE` is a subclass of `ValueError`; the fact that compaction's handler had to be changed at all is evidence that it is a distinct exception type. If it is not a `ValueError` subclass, then `_age_days("garbage", "2024-01-01")` (and `clock.parse_date(newest)` in `kind_worklog` when `newest` is malformed) propagates `clock.UNPARSEABLE` out of the `try` instead of returning `None` / `""`, turning a single malformed date into an unhandled exception that aborts the whole export. Either `UNPARSEABLE` must derive from `ValueError` or these two handlers must catch `clock.UNPARSEABLE` like compaction does.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/kind_bugs.py:43 and ddflow/services/export/kind_worklog.py:88

chunk_findings.detail: `_parse_time` was changed to `t = clock.parse_ts(text, naive="local")` but still handles failure with `except ValueError as exc: raise QuotaError(...)`. `clock.parse_ts` signals an unparseable string via `clock.UNPARSEABLE`, not `ValueError` — the identical switch from `except ValueError` to `except clock.UNPARSEABLE` was required at the `services/triggers.py::ts` call site of the same function in this change, which is why that handler was rewritten. A malformed anchor coming from config (e.g. `_parse_time("yesterday")`, or an empty string) therefore raises `clock.UNPARSEABLE` straight out of the service instead of the intended `QuotaError("anchor ... is not an ISO-8601 time")`, so the user sees an unhandled traceback instead of the clean quota error the function is supposed to produce. (The same pattern applies to the `except ValueError` around `clock.parse_date` in `services/export/query.py` if `parse_date` shares that failure type.)
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/quota.py:_parse_time

chunk_findings.detail: The new `time_parse` counter only inspects calls whose `func` is an `ast.Attribute`, so a timestamp parsed through a directly imported name is never counted, even though it is exactly what `tests/guard_baselines/time_parse.toml` claims to forbid ("counts fromisoformat or strptime outside ddflow.core.clock"). Given a file such as `ddflow/core/foo.py` containing `from time import strptime` followed by `def f(s): return strptime(s, "%Y-%m-%d")`, the `Call` node's `func` is an `ast.Name`, not an `ast.Attribute`, so `self.sites["time_parse"]` stays empty for that file; the total remains 0 and the new baseline of 0 passes, while a `strptime` call has been introduced outside `ddflow.core.clock`. Adding `ast.Name` handling for names bound to `time.strptime` (or rejecting direct imports of those names) would close the hole.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_architecture_guards.py:215 (`_TIME_PARSERS` branch in `visit_Call`)

chunk_findings.detail: The function is declared as `def test_every_helper_returns_what_it_returned_before_the_move(shape, *"abcdefg"):`. In a `def` parameter list the token after `*` must be a `NAME` (a `star_parameter`); a string literal is not a legal parameter name, so `def f(shape, *"abcdefg")` is a `SyntaxError`, not a valid varargs declaration. The `*"abcdefg"` unpacking trick is only legal where it is used a line above, inside the tuple literal passed to `@pytest.mark.parametrize`. Consequence: `tests/test_clock.py` cannot be compiled/imported, so pytest reports a collection error and *every* pinned assertion in the module is skipped (none of the old-parser behaviours are actually pinned). Even if the parser accepted it, the body references `a`…`g` as bare names, which would then be `NameError`s, since the varargs value would be bound to a single argument. The signature must be spelled out explicitly, e.g. `(shape, a, b, c, d, e, f, g)`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_clock.py:test_every_helper_returns_what_it_returned_before_the_move

chunk_findings.detail: That row contains eight values after the shape (`0.0, 0.0, INF, INF, None, "2026-10-07T01:02:03+00:00", "!QuotaError", None`), whereas the parametrization argnames `("shape", *"abcdefg")` and the `got` tuple in the body both expect exactly seven (`progress.epoch`, `records._epoch`, `sessions._age_s`, `_iso(triggers.ts)`, `query._parse_ts`, `quota._parse_time`, `kind_bugs._age_days`). Every other row (including the otherwise-equivalent `"garbage"` and `""` rows) has seven. With the extra `INF`, pytest cannot bind the row to the eight names / the test would receive nine values, so this case fails to run at all; the intended value for this shape is almost certainly `(0.0, 0.0, INF, None, "2026-10-07T01:02:03+00:00", "!QuotaError", None)` (the whitespace-padded string is unparseable for triggers/sessions but query strips it), i.e. one `INF` is spurious and shifts the rest of the columns.

chunk_findings.detail: The new core/clock parsers report parse failures by raising `clock.UNPARSEABLE` — that is exactly why the sibling call site in `ddflow/services/compaction.py:114` was changed from `except ValueError` to `except clock.UNPARSEABLE`. These two date-based call sites were left catching `ValueError`, so the failure contract no longer matches. `clock.UNPARSEABLE` is not a `ValueError`, so the handler is dead. Concretely: `_age_days(found="", until="2024-01-01")` used to take the `ValueError` branch produced by `date.fromisoformat("")` and return `None`; now `clock.parse_date("")` raises `clock.UNPARSEABLE`, which `except ValueError` does not catch, so the exception escapes `_age_days` and aborts the whole bug export instead of returning `None`. The identical change in `kind_worklog` (`clock.parse_date(newest)` inside `except ValueError`) has the same defect for any `days` entry that is not a clean ISO date, turning the previous `return ""` fallback into a propagated exception. The fix is to catch `clock.UNPARSEABLE` (or ensure the clock module makes it a `ValueError` subclass); as written, the two callers regress from graceful degradation to crashing.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/kind_bugs.py:43 (also ddflow/services/export/kind_worklog.py:88)

chunk_findings.detail: The date check replaced `datetime.fromisoformat(...)` with `clock.parse_date(...)`, but the branch it feeds is not date-only. For any `since` of length ≥ `_DATE_LEN` the whole string (not a truncated 10-char date) is forwarded to the parser — that is exactly the long branch, and `_DATE_PREFIX` is a *prefix* match (proved by the short branch that exists to pad partial dates such as `2024` / `2024-06`), so strings carrying a time component reach this call. The original `datetime.fromisoformat` accepted both dates and timestamps — as the error text on the line above advertises ("is not an ISO date or timestamp") — whereas `clock.parse_date`, named for and implemented around `date.fromisoformat` (the very `fromisoformat` the new ratchet pins inside `core/clock`), accepts only date-only strings. Concretely, `ddflow ... --since 2024-06-01T09:30:00` (len 19 ≥ `_DATE_LEN`) previously validated and was used; now `parse_date("2024-06-01T09:30:00")` raises `ValueError`, which the surrounding `except ValueError` converts into `ExportError("--since '2024-06-01T09:30:00' is not a real date", EXIT_REFUSED)`, refusing a command that used to run. The fix is to call a clock helper that parses date-or-datetime (e.g. pass the date portion, or use the same `parse_ts`-style function with `naive` handling) rather than the date-only parser.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/query.py:170 (`_parse_since`, `clock.parse_date`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The entry for the padded shape has **nine** elements, not eight:

```python
    (
        " 2026-10-07T01:02:03Z ",   # shape
        0.0,                        # a progress.epoch
        0.0,                        # b records._epoch
        INF,                        # c sessions._age_s
        INF,                        # <-- extra
        None,                       # ?
        "2026-10-07T01:02:03+00:00",# ?
        "!QuotaError",              # ?
        None,                       # <-- extra
    ),
```

Every other row (e.g. the `+0000` row, the `2026-10-07` row, `"garbage"`, `""`) carries exactly `shape + 7` values, and the test is declared with `@pytest.mark.parametrize(("shape", *"abcdefg"), PINNED, ...)`, i.e. 8 argnames (`shape`, `a`..`g`). A row with 8 values breaks that contract, so pytest fails during **collection** of `tests/test_clock.py` with an argnames/values arity error and none of the tests in this file (including the module-level `now_iso`/`parse_ts`/`parse_date` tests, which are unrelated to this row) ever run.

The row is also internally inconsistent even if the arity were patched by deleting one element: position `d` is compared against `_iso(triggers.ts(shape))`, and `_iso` returns only a string or `None` (`t.isoformat() if t else None`), so a pinned float `INF` can never be the result of that call for any input; likewise `g` for the padded shape is pinned to `"!QuotaError"` while the otherwise analogous unparseable rows (`garbage`, `""`) pin `kind_bugs._age_days` to `None`. The row needs to be rewritten as `shape + 7` values.

chunk_findings.detail: The `try` body now calls `clock.parse_date(...)`, but the handler is still `except ValueError`. In this same change, the sibling call site that switches to a clock parser (`ddflow/services/compaction.py`, `except clock.UNPARSEABLE`) deliberately stops catching `ValueError`, which is only meaningful if `clock.UNPARSEABLE` is *not* a subclass of `ValueError`. If `clock.parse_date` reports malformed input the same way its timestamp sibling does, then `_age_days("garbage", "2024-01-01")` no longer falls into the handler; `clock.UNPARSEABLE` propagates out of `_age_days` instead of returning `None`, and the bugs export view blows up on a bug whose `found`/`until` string is not a parseable date, where previously it degraded to `None` (and thus no age shown). The two call sites cannot both be right: either compaction should keep catching `ValueError`, or these two should catch `clock.UNPARSEABLE`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/kind_bugs.py:43 (`_age_days`)

chunk_findings.detail: Identical inconsistency: the `try` block calls `clock.parse_date(newest)` but the handler remains `except ValueError`. Given that the change rewrote the equivalent clock-parser guard in `compaction.latest` to `except clock.UNPARSEABLE`, a malformed `newest` (e.g. a `days` entry such as `"2024-13-40"`) escapes as `clock.UNPARSEABLE` rather than being caught and turned into the previous `""` window-start result, so the worklog export raises instead of rendering an empty window. Either the exception type used by `clock.parse_date` differs from the one assumed here, or this handler (and the one in `kind_bugs`) was missed when the parsers were moved onto `clock`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/kind_worklog.py:88

chunk_findings.detail: The old code validated `since` with `datetime.fromisoformat(...)`, and note that the branch passes `since` *verbatim* whenever it is at least `_DATE_LEN` characters long (`... if len(since) < _DATE_LEN else since`). Since `_DATE_PREFIX` already guarantees a `YYYY-MM-DD` prefix, that `else` branch is the one that actually runs for every accepted value, and it is reached with full timestamps as well as bare dates. `clock.parse_date` is the date parser (the clock's timestamp parser is `clock.parse_ts`, used just above in `_parse_ts`), so given `--since 2024-05-01T10:00:00` it will not accept the time component and raises, after which the `except ValueError` turns it into `ExportError("--since ... is not a real date", EXIT_REFUSED)`. The previous `datetime.fromisoformat("2024-05-01T10:00:00")` accepted that input, so exported ranges specified as timestamps are now refused — a behavior regression, not just a refactor. The validation must go through `clock.parse_ts` (or `parse_date` must be defined to accept datetimes).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/query.py:170 (the `clock.parse_date(...)` validation line)

chunk_findings.detail:
The second half of the new condition only fires when the callee is an `ast.Name` *and* `"." in name`. But the case the comment and the new test explicitly promise to cover is `from time import strptime` followed by `strptime(s, f)`: there the callee is a bare `ast.Name` whose identifier is `strptime`, i.e. `name == "strptime"` with no dot, so the `"." in name` conjunct is False and the site is never appended to `self.sites["time_parse"]`. The new parametrized case added at line 547 (`"from time import strptime
from datetime import datetime as dt
strptime(s, f)
dt.fromisoformat(a)
fromisoformat = 1
"`, expected `2`) consequently records only `dt.fromisoformat` and yields 1, not 2. More importantly, the ratchet this file is adding does not actually catch the documented bare-name form: a module can reintroduce `strptime` via `from time import strptime` and the `time_parse` baseline stays at 0, defeating the stated purpose of keeping parsing in `core.clock`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_architecture_guards.py:216 (the `time_parse` `ast.Name` branch in `visit_Call`)

chunk_findings.detail:
`naive="refuse"` is documented in the module docstring (lines 11-12) as the mode for quota anchors: "it is an error, because the same wall-clock time is a different moment on another machine." `parse_ts` does raise — it raises `NoTimezone`. But `NoTimezone` subclasses `ValueError` (line 34), and `ValueError` is a member of `UNPARSEABLE` (line 31), so `epoch`'s `except UNPARSEABLE` swallows the refusal and returns `default`. `age_s` then hard-codes `default=float("inf")` (line 75), so it returns `+inf` instead of raising.

Concrete input: `clock.epoch("2026-10-07T01:02:03", naive="refuse")` returns `0.0` (1970-01-01), not `NoTimezone`; `clock.age_s("2026-10-07T01:02:03", naive="refuse", now=t)` returns `inf`. A quota-anchor caller that reads a zone-less timestamp through `epoch`/`age_s` therefore cannot obtain the refusal it explicitly asked for — it silently gets a bogus epoch (or "infinitely old"), which is precisely the silent-corruption outcome the `refuse` mode exists to prevent. The refusal is only reachable via the lower-level `parse_ts`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/clock.py:64-69 (epoch) and :72-78 (age_s)

chunk_findings.detail: `_age_days` now calls `clock.parse_date(...)` but still catches `ValueError`. The sibling change in `compaction.py` shows that the `clock` parsers report failure via `clock.UNPARSEABLE` (that is why `latest` was changed from `except ValueError` to `except clock.UNPARSEABLE`). If `clock.UNPARSEABLE` is not a `ValueError` subclass, then a bug record with a malformed date, e.g. `found="not-a-date"`, makes `clock.parse_date("not-a-date")` raise `clock.UNPARSEABLE`, which is not caught: the exception escapes `_age_days` and aborts the whole export, where the pre-change code returned `None` for exactly this case. The `try/except` here exists precisely because `found`/`until` are free-form fields, so this is a real regression, not a theoretical one.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/kind_bugs.py:43 (`_age_days`)

chunk_findings.detail:
Same defect: the code was switched to `clock.parse_date(newest)` but still uses `except ValueError`. Given a `newest` value that the new parser rejects, the `clock.UNPARSEABLE` (per the contract evidenced by `compaction.py`) propagates out of the function instead of the previous `return ""`. The original `date.fromisoformat` raised `ValueError`, which the handler caught; the replacement parser raises a different type, so the guard is now dead for the failure it was written for.

Both findings share the same root cause and the same fix (catch `clock.UNPARSEABLE`, as `compaction.py` was updated to do). I did not find a concrete defect in the `progress.py` or `compaction.py` hunks themselves beyond this.

chunk_findings.detail: The pinned row for the padded input `" 2026-10-07T01:02:03Z "` has nine elements, while `@pytest.mark.parametrize(("shape", *"abcdefg"), PINNED, ...)` declares eight parameters (`shape`, `a`–`g`) and the test function accepts eight. pytest requires each `PINNED` entry to have exactly the declared arity, so collecting `tests/test_clock.py` errors out ("expected 8 arguments, got 9") and the whole module fails before any of the pinned-parser guarantees are exercised. The row is also self-inconsistent independent of the arity check: its `triggers.ts` column is pinned to `INF`, but that column is produced by `_iso(triggers.ts(shape))`, which can only ever yield an `isoformat()` string or `None`; and its `query._parse_ts` column is pinned to `None`, but that column is produced by `query._parse_ts(shape).isoformat()` wrapped in `_call`, which can only ever yield a string (a `None` parse result would raise `AttributeError` and become `"!AttributeError"`). So for this input the assertion is guaranteed to fail even if the arity problem is fixed by trimming a value.

chunk_findings.detail: `longest_chains` is the only walk in the module with no cycle guard: `topological_order` raises `graphlib.CycleError`, `transitive_reduction` inherits that guard, `find_cycles` is the diagnoser, and `closure` is guarded by `seen`. `longest_chains` has none, so it does not terminate (the stack grows without bound) on a cyclic input. Concretely, `longest_chains(["a", "b"], before)` with `before(a) == ["b"]` and `before(b) == ["a"]` pushes `(a, [b], 0)`, then `(b, [a], 0)`, then `(a, [b], 0)` again forever — each node is re-pushed because `memo` is only written in the post-order pop, never marked "in progress". This is exactly the failure mode the module docstring says is impossible ("every walk is cycle-guarded, because the code that walks it is also the code that diagnoses bad plans") and exactly the guard/walk mismatch `find_cycles`' own docstring warns about: if the caller's `find_cycles` traversed a different relation (e.g. the default `it.needs`) than the relation `longest_chains` walks (e.g. inherited dependencies), the guard returns "acyclic" while `longest_chains` hangs / exhausts memory instead of refusing the plan. The walk should either raise on a cycle or the docstring/guard contract should be enforced, not left to each call site.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/graph.py:longest_chains

chunk_findings.detail: `Item.ancestors` previously returned its result in a guaranteed order — the hand-rolled loop walked one parent at a time, so the list was nearest-first, exactly as the (unchanged) docstring promises ("The parent chain above ``item_id``, nearest first"). The new body is `[self.items[n] for n in closure(item_id, parent) if n != item_id]`, which returns the ancestors in whatever order `closure` happens to iterate, and the sibling rewrites in the same diff treat `closure` as producing an unordered collection (both `records.descendants` and `progress` wrap it in `set(...)`, and the loops it replaces built `seen: set[str]` and returned that set). Concretely, for items `c` (parent `b`) and `b` (parent `a`), the old code yielded `[b, a]`; the new code yields `list(<closure result>)`, which for a set-returning closure is hash-based — and since these are `str`, that order varies from process to process under hash randomization. Any caller that takes the immediate parent as `ancestors(x)[0]`, or that renders/compares the chain in order, now gets the grandparent (or an arbitrary ancestor) first, nondeterministically. The property tests against networkx won't catch this because networkx's `ancestors` returns an unordered set, so the loss of the documented ordering is invisible to the oracle.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/records.py:917 (Item.ancestors)

chunk_findings.detail:
The rewritten `_depth` recovers the old "self-parent counts one extra step" quirk by inspecting `above[-1]` — i.e. it assumes the self-parenting node is the *last* element that `closure()` yields. That assumption only holds if `closure()` returns items in traversal/chain order. If `closure()` returns a `set` (which is what the networkx oracle the change is property-tested against produces for `ancestors`/`descendants`, and the natural implementation here), `above[-1]` is an arbitrary element and the self-loop bonus is silently dropped whenever the self-parent node is not the last set element.

Concrete input that demonstrates it (a chain that ends in a self-parent):

    state.items = {
        "a": item(id="a", parent="b"),
        "b": item(id="b", parent="c"),
        "c": item(id="c", parent="c"),   # self-parent
    }
    root = ""

Old code returns 3 (`a`→`b`→`c`→`c`, the terminal `c` counted twice). New code computes `closure("a", parent) == {"a","b","c"}`; filtering gives `above`, but if the set iterates as `["c","b"]` then `last = state.items["b"]`, `last.parent ("c") == last.id ("b")` is `False`, so the result is `min(2 + 0, 6) == 2` instead of `3` — an off-by-one in rendered depth that depends on `PYTHONHASHSEED`/set iteration order (i.e. flaky across runs and environments). Conversely `["b","c"]` gives the correct 3. Any chain with a deeper self-parent and more than one ancestor (e.g. `a→b→c→d→d`) is exposed the same way.

The fix is to detect the self-loop independently of iteration order (e.g. `any(state.items[n].parent == n and n != root for n in above)`, or have the closure walk expose its terminal), not to read `above[-1]`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/views/markdown.py `_depth` (the `above`/`last`/`return min(...)` lines)

chunk_findings.detail: `digraphs` builds `adj[a]` as a's successors and `nx_of` turns each `b in adj[a]` into the edge `a→b`, which the closure test relies on when it compares `G.closure(s, lambda n: adj[n])` with `nx.descendants` — so `adj[a]` is unambiguously a's successors. A topological order must then put every predecessor first, i.e. for every edge a→b, `pos[a] < pos[b]`, which is exactly what the test's own name ("puts every predecessor first") claims. The assertion inverts this: `pos[b] < pos[a]` requires the *successor* to appear before its predecessor. On the smallest input the strategy can draw, `adj = {"n0": ["n1"], "n1": []}`, it demands `pos["n1"] < pos["n0"]`, i.e. n1 first, the reverse of a topological order. So against a correct `G.topological_order` (predecessors first) this test fails on essentially every non-empty graph, and if it instead passes it is because `topological_order` really returns a reversed/successors-first order — a wrong result that this assertion bakes in, leaving the whole suite unable to detect it. The comparison should be `pos[a] < pos[b]`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_core_graph.py::test_topological_order_puts_every_predecessor_first (assertion `pos[b] < pos[a]`)

chunk_findings.detail: The docstring promises "Every dependency cycle, each reported once, starting at its smallest id", but the function only records the *fundamental* cycle of each DFS back edge (edge into a GREY node). Cycles that close via a cross/forward edge are never enumerated, because when such an edge is examined the target is already BLACK and is silently skipped. Concrete input: items `{"a","b","c"}` with `edges(a)=["b","c"]`, `edges(b)=["c","a"]`, `edges(c)=["a"]` (i.e. a→b, a→c, b→c, b→a, c→a). Tracing the DFS: pick `a`, pop `c` first, `c→a` is a back edge → `[a,c,a]`; then `b→a` is a back edge → `[a,b,a]`. The three-node cycle `a→b→c→a` (a needs b, b needs c, c needs a) is a genuine dependency cycle but is never returned, because `b→c` is a forward edge and `c` is BLACK when it is examined. `networkx.simple_cycles` returns all three, so a networkx-oracle test would disagree; the property tests are stated to run "on random DAGs", which cannot exercise this path. For a health-check that exists to diagnose bad plans this means the reported cycle set can be a strict subset of the real one (fixing exactly the reported cycles can leave the plan cyclic).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/graph.py `find_cycles` (the `found.append(cyc[lo:] + cyc[:lo] + [cyc[lo]])` enumeration)

chunk_findings.detail: The docstring states "The parent chain above ``item_id``, nearest first", and the previous implementation preserved that order by appending each parent as it walked up the chain. The new implementation returns `[self.items[n] for n in closure(item_id, parent) if n != item_id]`, i.e. it materializes a list by iterating the `closure` result. `closure` is the shared reachability primitive used by `descendants` (wrapped in `set(...)`) and tested against networkx's set-returning `descendants`/`ancestors`, so it returns an unordered set. Iterating that set gives hash-bucket order, not chain order. Concretely, for a chain `item -> A -> B` (A parent of item, B parent of A), `closure(item, parent)` is `{A, B}` and the returned list may be `[B, A]` instead of `[A, B]`. Any caller that relies on the documented contract — e.g. taking `ancestors(item)[0]` to get the immediate parent, or rendering the chain nearest-first — now receives an arbitrary ancestor and an arbitrary order. (The property tests would not catch this, since networkx's `ancestors` returns a set and the comparison is therefore order-insensitive.)
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/records.py:~908 (`Item.ancestors`)

chunk_findings.detail: The replacement successor lambda drops both guards the recursion it replaces performed: `if dep in items` and `items[dep].state != DONE`. `items` still contains finished items (that is exactly why `open_ids` is computed as a separate non-DONE list), so a completed dependency is now traversed and becomes part of the chain. Concretely, with `items = {P: phase (open), T: task (state DONE)}` and `before(P) == ["T"]`, the old `longest("P", frozenset())` skipped `T` and produced `["P"]`; the new `longest_chains([...P...], lambda n: before(items[n]))` walks into `T` and yields `["T", "P"]`, so the reported floor is longer than before and `max(chains, key=len)` returns a chain containing completed work — defeating the stated purpose of the number ("stop someone adding a fifth agent to a phase whose runtime is set by a chain"). The same lambda also no longer protects the lookup: `before()` can return ids that are not keys of `items` (the reason the old `dep in items` check existed, and the reason the sibling `closure(...)` lambda in the same hunk filters `d in live`), so `items[n]` raises `KeyError` for such a dependency instead of skipping it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/schedule.py — `longest = longest_chains(open_ids, lambda n: before(items[n]))`

chunk_findings.detail:
The rewritten `_depth` assumes that the last element of `above` is the terminal node of the parent chain:

```python
above = [n for n in closure(item.id, parent) if n != item.id]
last = state.items[above[-1]] if above else item
return min(len(above) + (last.parent == last.id != root), 6)
```

`above` is built by iterating whatever `closure(item.id, parent)` returns. `closure` is the ancestor/descendant closure introduced by this change and is property-tested against networkx's `ancestors`/`descendants`, i.e. it has set semantics and gives no guarantee that its iteration order is the walk order (item → parent → grandparent → …). The old code obtained the chain terminal deterministically by walking `node.parent`; the new code infers it from iteration position.

Concrete failing input: `root = "P"`, and `state.items = {"a": item(parent="b"), "b": item(parent="s"), "s": item(parent="s")}` — the chain `a → b → s → s`, where `s` is its own parent (the exact case the docstring/comment says must be handled). The old `_depth` walks `a→b` (depth 1), `b→s` (depth 2), then `s→s` because `s` is not yet in `seen` (depth 3), then stops; it returns 3. The new code computes `above = list(closure("a", parent)) \ {"a"}`. If the closure yields the set `{"b", "s"}` in the order `["s", "b"]` (set/hash order is unspecified and can vary with the ids in a real project), then `above[-1]` is `"b"`, `last.parent` is `"s"`, which is not `last.id` (`"b"`), so the `+1` self-parent compensation is skipped and `_depth` returns `2` instead of `3`. The rendered depth for the same item therefore depends on unspecified iteration order of `closure`'s result rather than on the chain itself; whenever the chain terminates in a self-parent node and there is at least one intermediate ancestor, the `+1` in the last line is only applied if that terminal node happens to be iterated last.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/views/markdown.py:_depth

chunk_findings.detail: The property asserts `pos[b] < pos[a]` for every edge `a -> b` (`for a, bs in adj.items() for b in bs`). But the `digraphs` strategy defines `adj` as `{node: [successor, ...]}`, and the sibling helper `_longest_from` walks `g.successors`/`nx_of` builds edges exactly `a -> b for b in adj[a]`; so `b` is a successor of `a` and `a` is its predecessor. The assertion therefore requires every successor to come *before* its predecessor, i.e. a reversed topological order — the opposite of what the test name claims. Concretely, for `adj = {"a": ["b"]}` a correct `topological_order` returns `["a", "b"]`, giving `pos["a"]=0 < pos["b"]=1`, so `pos["b"] < pos["a"]` fails; if the assertion instead passes, it is pinning an inverted order for a function whose argument is interpreted as forward edges everywhere else in the same file (`G.closure(s, lambda n: adj[n])` is compared against `nx.descendants`, which follows `adj` forward). Either the assertion is wrong (test fails against a correct implementation) or it certifies a reversed/inconsistent `topological_order`; both are defects. Note this is not merely a naming issue: the assertion is the executable spec for the ordering direction.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_core_graph.py::test_topological_order_puts_every_predecessor_first

Probe: needs {n0:[n3,n1], n1:[n0], n2:[n0,n2], n3:[n1]} -> [[n0,n1,n0],[n2,n2]], but n3 is on n0->n3->n1->n0 (networkx strongly_connected_components). 304 of 20000 random graphs on 2-6 nodes miss at least one cyclic item. Found by the B-uni-graph critic review (deepseek).
