chunk_findings.detail: The prior finding still holds because this diff does not fix it — the triage "answers" it by filing `Bfdaf61894b`/`fix-Bfdaf61894b`, which changes nothing in the code under review, and the enumeration logic shown here is still back-edge-only: a `dep` whose colour is BLACK is silently skipped (`elif c == WHITE` is the only branch that descends), so cycles that close through a cross/forward edge are never found, contradicting the docstring's "Every dependency cycle, each reported once". Concretely, `find_cycles({n0:[n3,n1], n1:[n0], n2:[n0,n2], n3:[n1]})` returns `[[n0,n1,n0],[n2,n2]]`: processing `n0`, the DFS pops `n1` (LIFO from `[n3,n1]`) and reports `n0→n1→n0`; `n1` is then popped and marked BLACK, so when `n3` is later explored its edge `n3→n1` hits a BLACK node and the genuine cycle `n0→n3→n1→n0` is never emitted. Since `find_cycles` is the cycle source for `schedule`, a plan whose only cycle runs through such an edge passes the guard, after which `longest_chains`/critical-path can return a confidently wrong result or the walk can disagree with the health check that is supposed to reject bad plans.

chunk_findings.detail: This is the previously reported MEDIUM finding, still present. The docstring promises "Every dependency cycle, each reported once, starting at its smallest id", but the routine only records the fundamental cycle of each DFS back edge (edge into a GREY node); a cycle whose closing edge lands on a BLACK node is silently skipped. Because the triage was `confirmed` only by *filing* fix-Bfdaf61894b and the function was moved verbatim (nothing in this diff changes the code), the newly consolidated cycle source still under-reports. Callers that use this as the cycle source (cycle reporting under `cycle_policy="warn"`) can therefore present a cyclic schedule to the user with a strict subset of its cycles. A filed follow-up task does not answer the finding in this change; the code must actually enumerate cycles through both back and cross/forward edges (or the docstring/contract must be narrowed).

chunk_findings.detail: `find_cycles` promises "Every dependency cycle, each reported once, starting at its smallest id", but the 3‑colour DFS only reports one cycle per blackened node set, so it silently drops cycles that merge into an already‑finished node. Concrete input: `items = {a,b,c,d}` with `edges = {a:[b,c], b:[d], c:[d], d:[a]}`. From root `a` the DFS pops `c` first (LIFO `pending.pop()`), walks `a→c→d`, sees `d→a` (a is GREY) and reports `[a,c,d,a]`. `d` and `c` are then marked BLACK; when `b→d` is explored, `d` is BLACK, so the second elementary cycle `a→b→d→a` is never reported. `networkx.simple_cycles` returns both. The docstring/contract says both should be emitted; any caller (the health/diagnosis path that is "the cycle source") that enumerates cycles to show the user all offending dependency loops gets an incomplete list. Note this is not covered by the Hypothesis oracle, which is run on random DAGs. If "one cycle per SCC" is in fact the intended contract, the docstring overclaims and should be narrowed; as written the function does not do what it says.

chunk_findings.detail: The refactor drops the old per-dependency guard `if dep in items and items[dep].state != DONE`. The replaced memoised `longest` walked `before(it)` but only followed predecessors that were themselves still open, so a finished dependency could not appear in a chain. The new callback `lambda n: before(items[n])` returns *every* predecessor, DONE ones included, and the only filtering the caller does is `open_ids = [i for i, it in items.items() if it.state != DONE]`, which selects the *keys* of the returned mapping, not the traversal. So the DONE filter now rests entirely on the unstated assumption that `longest_chains` internally restricts `before()` to the ids it is handed; the sibling `closure` call two lines above needed an explicit `[d for d in before(live[n]) if d in live]` for exactly the same reason, so calling `before` unfiltered is not how this module is used elsewhere. Concrete failure: with `items = {P: open, D: DONE}` and `before(items[P]) == ["D"]` (P depends on completed D), the old code computed the chain `["P"]` for P; the new code computes `["D", "P"]` unless `longest_chains` discards D. `max(chains, key=len)` then reports a floor one longer than the work remaining — it re-counts finished work, which contradicts the preserved comment that this number "exists precisely to stop someone adding a fifth agent to a phase whose runtime is set by a chain." The property tests against networkx would not catch this, because the oracle is exercised with the full node set, where subset filtering is a no-op.

chunk_findings.detail:
The cycle list is emitted backwards. `stack` descends from a node into its `before` predecessors: when `n` is on top, `p = preds[i]` is a prerequisite that gets pushed on top, so for consecutive stack entries `stack[k], stack[k+1]` the dependency edge points `stack[k+1] -> stack[k]` (deeper prerequisite → shallower dependent). A back edge to `p = stack[j]` (with current node `n = stack[-1]`) is therefore `p -> n`, and the real cycle is `p -> n -> stack[-2] -> … -> stack[j+1] -> p`. `[*path[path.index(p):], p]` instead emits `[p, stack[j+1], …, n, p]`, i.e. the reverse traversal.

Concrete input: `before(b)=[a]`, `before(c)=[b]`, `before(a)=[c]` (edges a→b, b→c, c→a). A DFS starting at `a` gives `path=[a,b,c]`, `path.index(a)=0`, so the code raises `CycleError(..., [a, c, b, a])`. Consecutive entries of that list (`a→c`, `c→b`, `b→a`) are not dependencies at all — the edge-following cycle is `[a, b, c, a]`. This contradicts the comment's stated "graphlib's shape" (graphlib reports the cycle so that consecutive nodes are connected by edges), and it also contradicts the same diff's `_shortest_cycle`, which returns edge-following cycles via `path[::-1]`. Any consumer or property test that walks the reported cycle pairwise, or compares it against graphlib/networkx output for the same graph, sees a reversed (or, for its pairwise edges, invalid) cycle.

chunk_findings.detail: On an acyclic graph — the normal, healthy input — `found` is empty, so `named` is empty and the new loop runs `_shortest_cycle(n, items, edge)` for *every* node. Each call is a fresh BFS over everything reachable from `n`, invoking `edge(items[...])` on every visited node. For a linear plan of V modules (each depending on the previous, no cycles), this is Σᵢ i = Θ(V²) BFS visits and `edge()` calls: ~12.5M for 5 000 modules and ~200M for 20 000. The module's own docstring notes the dependency-chain length is "operator-authored and therefore unbounded," so this is exactly the input shape it must tolerate — yet a previously linear health check becomes quadratic (worse if `edge()` parses strings), and can effectively hang on large plans. The DFS pass already yields O(V+E) when acyclic; the fallback should only be reached when a cycle is known to exist, not on every healthy plan.

chunk_findings.detail: The cycle reported by `longest_chains` is now reversed relative to `graphlib.CycleError`. For a graph whose adjacency maps each node to its predecessors, e.g. `adj = {"s": ["a"], "a": ["b"], "b": ["s"]}`, the DFS stack is `[s, a, b]` and the back-edge target is `p = s`. The original code produced `[s, a, b, s]`, which matches graphlib. The added test asserts the reversed orientation (`a in adj[b]` with `adj` mapping predecessors) and incorrectly claims this is graphlib's orientation. Callers that parse `CycleError.args[1]` expecting graphlib's shape will now see every edge reversed.

chunk_findings.detail: The token was `f"{os.getpid()}-{time.time_ns()}"`, which is unique per lock acquisition. It is now `f"{os.getpid()}-{clock.run_stamp()}"`. `run_stamp` is, by the change's own description, a stamp for the *run* (`"run_stamp for run and file ids"`), i.e. it is stable for the life of the process/run rather than fresh per call. The token's stated purpose is to let a holder recognize that a lock "is no longer its own", which requires the token written by one acquisition to differ from the token written by the next. With a constant `run_stamp()` and an unchanged `os.getpid()`, every acquisition made by a given process now writes the *identical* token; only the pid still separates different concurrent processes, and the pid is the same for every acquisition inside one process. Concretely: a process acquires lock `L` (writes token `"<pid>-<stamp>"`), releases it (removes the file), and later re-acquires `L` (same file identity, same `"<pid>-<stamp>"`). Any late/duplicate release still carrying the first acquisition's token now compares equal to the current lock file and deletes the *live* second acquisition's lock, letting a third party proceed while the second holder is still inside the critical section. Under the old `time.time_ns()` the two tokens differed, so the stale release was correctly ignored. The same collision lets two threads of one process contending for `L` treat each other's lock as their own. (Cross-process contention is still separated by the pid, so the regression is intra-process: repeated/duplicate acquisition by the same process yields interchangeable tokens.)
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/flowstate.py:147 (lock token)

chunk_findings.detail: This test builds `same = {clock.run_stamp(at) for _ in range(5000)}` and asserts `len(same) == 5000`. `run_stamp`'s default token is 8 hex characters (the `STAMP` regex requires exactly `[0-9a-f]{8}`, and `run_stamp(at, token_hex=5)` yields a 5-char token), i.e. a 32-bit random space. The expected number of colliding pairs is C(5000,2)/2^32 ≈ 12497500/4294967296 ≈ 0.0029, so the assertion fails roughly once every ~344 runs of the test — a nondeterministic, flaky failure that has nothing to do with the code under test. Since the test's stated purpose is to pin that stamps made in one second are distinct, either the sample count must be reduced or the default token sized so that collisions are negligible (or uniqueness within a second must be guaranteed rather than drawn from a 32-bit space).

chunk_findings.detail: `run_stamp` fixes the timestamp at one-second resolution and leaves the discriminating part of the name (the 8 random hex digits) unordered, so two names minted in the same second do **not** sort in creation order — directly contradicting the docstring's stated purpose ("The time makes names sort in the order they were made, on every machine"). For the job log this is a regression, not just a doc nit: the code this replaces used `time.time_ns()`, whose suffix was monotonic, so two launches for one item in the same second produced `item-1712345678901234567.log` and `item-1712345678901234568.log`, ordered newest-last. After the change the same two launches produce, say, `item-20261007T010203Z-bbbbbbbb.log` and `item-20261007T010203Z-aaaaaaaa.log`, whose lexicographic order is decided by the random token. Any consumer that recovers the newest run/log by taking the lexicographic maximum of an item's names (the property the timestamp prefix exists to provide, and the reason the review path's run id was second-stamped at all) will pick the older launch roughly half the time when two launches fall in the same second. Keeping a monotonic component in the suffix (e.g. `time_ns()` in addition to the token), or restricting the ordering claim in the docstring to cross-second comparisons, would remove the mismatch.

chunk_findings.detail:
The docstring on this function states the token exists so a holder does not remove "a lock that is no longer its own." That property depends on every acquisition producing a token that distinguishes it from any other acquisition of the same lock file. `time.time_ns()` gave that uniqueness per call. `clock.run_stamp()` is, per the change intent, a *run*-scoped stamp ("run_stamp for run and file ids") — a value that is fixed for the lifetime of the process/run. The token therefore collapses to a constant `f"{pid}-<run stamp>"` for **every** acquisition made by a given process.

Because the token was reduced to a per-process constant, the same-process case is no longer protected. Concrete interleaving in one process, two threads, same lock path:

1. T1 acquires the lock and holds it longer than the stale threshold (slow disk / GC pause / SIGSTOP).
2. T2's wait loop observes the file older than the stale age, unlinks it, and creates a fresh lock. Its token is `f"{pid}-{run_stamp}"` — byte-identical to T1's, since both threads share the pid and the run-scoped stamp. With the old token it would have been `f"{pid}-{<different ns>}"`.
3. T1 finishes and its release path reads the token, finds it equal to its own, and unlinks T2's lock file.
4. A third acquirer can now take the lock while T2 still believes it holds it, so two writers enter the critical section the lock is supposed to serialize.

Across processes the pid component still differs, which is presumably why this looks harmless in the "ordinary case" the docstring mentions — but the protection is no longer a property of the acquisition, only of the process, so any same-process steal (the exact "no longer its own" situation) is now indistinguishable.

chunk_findings.detail: The token was `f"{os.getpid()}-{time.time_ns()}"`, which is unique per lock acquisition. It is now `f"{os.getpid()}-{clock.run_stamp()}"`. `run_stamp` is, by the change's own description, a stamp for the *run* (`"run_stamp for run and file ids"`), i.e. it is stable for the life of the process/run rather than fresh per call. The token's stated purpose is to let a holder recognize that a lock "is no longer its own", which requires the token written by one acquisition to differ from the token written by the next. With a constant `run_stamp()` and an unchanged `os.getpid()`, every acquisition made by a given process now writes the *identical* token; only the pid still separates different concurrent processes, and the pid is the same for every acquisition inside one process. Concretely: a process acquires lock `L` (writes token `"<pid>-<stamp>"`), releases it (removes the file), and later re-acquires `L` (same file identity, same `"<pid>-<stamp>"`). Any late/duplicate release still carrying the first acquisition's token now compares equal to the current lock file and deletes the *live* second acquisition's lock, letting a third party proceed while the second holder is still inside the critical section. Under the old `time.time_ns()` the two tokens differed, so the stale release was correctly ignored. The same collision lets two threads of one process contending for `L` treat each other's lock as their own. (Cross-process contention is still separated by the pid, so the regression is intra-process: repeated/duplicate acquisition by the same process yields interchangeable tokens.)
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/flowstate.py:147 (lock token)

chunk_findings.detail: This test builds `same = {clock.run_stamp(at) for _ in range(5000)}` and asserts `len(same) == 5000`. `run_stamp`'s default token is 8 hex characters (the `STAMP` regex requires exactly `[0-9a-f]{8}`, and `run_stamp(at, token_hex=5)` yields a 5-char token), i.e. a 32-bit random space. The expected number of colliding pairs is C(5000,2)/2^32 ≈ 12497500/4294967296 ≈ 0.0029, so the assertion fails roughly once every ~344 runs of the test — a nondeterministic, flaky failure that has nothing to do with the code under test. Since the test's stated purpose is to pin that stamps made in one second are distinct, either the sample count must be reduced or the default token sized so that collisions are negligible (or uniqueness within a second must be guaranteed rather than drawn from a 32-bit space).
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_clock_stamps.py — test_run_stamps_made_in_one_second_differ_and_sort_by_time

chunk_findings.detail: `run_stamp` fixes the timestamp at one-second resolution and leaves the discriminating part of the name (the 8 random hex digits) unordered, so two names minted in the same second do **not** sort in creation order — directly contradicting the docstring's stated purpose ("The time makes names sort in the order they were made, on every machine"). For the job log this is a regression, not just a doc nit: the code this replaces used `time.time_ns()`, whose suffix was monotonic, so two launches for one item in the same second produced `item-1712345678901234567.log` and `item-1712345678901234568.log`, ordered newest-last. After the change the same two launches produce, say, `item-20261007T010203Z-bbbbbbbb.log` and `item-20261007T010203Z-aaaaaaaa.log`, whose lexicographic order is decided by the random token. Any consumer that recovers the newest run/log by taking the lexicographic maximum of an item's names (the property the timestamp prefix exists to provide, and the reason the review path's run id was second-stamped at all) will pick the older launch roughly half the time when two launches fall in the same second. Keeping a monotonic component in the suffix (e.g. `time_ns()` in addition to the token), or restricting the ordering claim in the docstring to cross-second comparisons, would remove the mismatch.

data.body:
A machine-readable manifest shipped in the wheel (ddflow/templates/upgrade/changes.toml) listing per release: new knobs (key, default, one-line why), CHANGED defaults (knob, old, new, behaviour effect), instruction/hook/template refreshes, repairs (ids), and opt-in features with the enabling command. Generated at release time from the log's complete --changelog lines + a lint that fails the release when config.py gained/changed a knob not listed (the dedupe warn->ask flip would have been caught). Reader API: changes_since(version).
Failing-first: a test diffs KNOB defaults between the previous tag and HEAD and requires a manifest entry for each added/changed knob; reading since 0.1.3 returns the 20 knobs found in the experiment. Docs shipped in templates; README section.

OPERATOR DECISION D-upgrade-manifest-lint (2026-10-03): the manifest lint BLOCKS a release by default ([release].manifest_lint = block|warn|off, default block, via config/CLI/MCP). A block prints the unmanifested changes and the operator's options: have an agent prepare the missing entries and safe-upgrade notes (pre-filled from the changelog fields and knob diff), waive named entries for this release with --waive <change> --reason (recorded), or change the policy. Agents may prepare and propose; waiving or lowering the policy is the operator's call. Failing-first test: a new knob with no entry blocks and prints the three options; a prepared entry passes; a waiver is recorded and shown in the next plan; warn and off do not block.

D-compat (operator 2026-10-06): part of P-unify's finish line (B-uni-acceptance needs it); P-unify's breaking changes are applied through it (B-uni-compat-migrations).

Split into: B-upgrade.2-changes.1-manifest, B-upgrade.2-changes.2-lint.

chunk_findings.detail: `_releases` iterates `data.get("release") or []` and immediately calls `rel.get(...)`, but — unlike `parse` (`isinstance(base, dict)`) and `_change` (`isinstance(raw, dict)`) — it never checks that each `rel` is a table. A manifest written with `[release]` instead of `[[release]]` parses to a dict for `data["release"]`, so `enumerate` yields the string keys (`"version"`, `"change"`), and `"version".get("version", "")` raises `AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get'`; likewise `release = ["0.2.0"]` crashes. The module docstring promises "ManifestError when either breaks the schema", and `load`/`changes_since`/`replay` propagate this, so callers that catch `ManifestError` for user-facing messages instead see an unhandled `AttributeError` on a plausible typo.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_manifest.py:_releases

chunk_findings.detail: The `why` recorded for this newly added knob is "Claims on a contended file are served first come, first served." That sentence describes claim ordering/queueing, not a value in seconds, and it is the only `knob_added` entry whose `why` neither names nor explains the knob it is attached to (e.g. contrast `schedule.adapt_cooldown_s` "Minimum seconds between two decreases… (default 300)"). A user upgrading to 0.1.10 and reading the entry for `lease.waiter_reservation_s = 300` therefore gets no information about what the 300-second reservation window does, and the text contradicts the knob's mechanism (a reservation duration is not a first-come-first-served rule). This reads as a backfill mis-attribution: the `why` was lifted from a different lease/claim-ordering commit than the one that introduced this key, so the manifest misinforms about the change it exists to document.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/upgrade/changes.toml:0.1.10 `[[release.change]] key = "lease.waiter_reservation_s"`

chunk_findings.detail: The `why` value is truncated mid-sentence: it ends with "plus the regression tests of the bugs it fixes -- and lists...", so the reader can never learn what the `selected` scope lists. The companion entry (`knob_added.gates.unit_tests_small_lines.toml`) has a complete, well-formed `why`, so the asymmetry is not a formatting convention of the manifest but a truncated value. Any consumer of `services/upgrade_manifest.changes_since(version)` that surfaces `why` to explain why `gates.unit_tests_scope` was added gets a dangling clause; and if the truncation comes from a length cap in `scripts/upgrade_manifest.py`, every long `why` is silently corrupted the same way (the "reproduces today's defaults" test only checks `new`, so it will not catch this).

chunk_findings.detail: `parse`'s docstring promises `ManifestError` "when either breaks the schema," and `_change` carefully guards `isinstance(raw, dict)` with a friendly message — but `_releases` never checks that each element of the `release` array is a table before calling `rel.get(...)`. Given a syntactically valid manifest such as `schema_version = 1` / `[base]` / `version = "0.1.3"` / `release = ["0.2.0"]` (or the single-table form `[release]` instead of `[[release]]`), `data.get("release")` is a list/dict of strings, `enumerate` yields the string `"0.2.0"` as `rel`, and `rel.get("version", "")` raises `AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get'` instead of `ManifestError`. A caller that catches `ManifestError` (the documented failure mode of `load`/`parse`) will not catch this, so a hand-edited or mis-typed shipped manifest crashes the reader with an unrelated exception. The same gap exists for `(base.get("knobs") or {}).items()` when `knobs` is a truthy non-table.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_manifest.py:_releases (`version = str(rel.get("version", ""))`)

chunk_findings.detail: The `why` value is truncated mid-sentence: it ends with `-- and lists...` after `plus the regression tests of the bugs it fixes -- and lists`. The sentence promises an enumeration ("and lists ...") that is never delivered, and there is no continuation line in the file (the file is exactly the 8 lines shown, per `@@ -0,0 +1,8 @@`). Since this string is the user-facing explanation surfaced by `services/upgrade_manifest.changes_since(version)` (and the README section), anyone reading the 0.1.3->next upgrade notes for the `gates.unit_tests_scope` knob gets a dangling, uninformative clause. Contrast with the sibling file `knob_added.gates.unit_tests_small_lines.toml:7`, whose `why` is a complete sentence, confirming this is an accidental cut, not a convention. No code path depends on the text, so impact is confined to the shipped explanation.

chunk_findings.detail: `assign_unreleased` folds the whole `unreleased` bucket into `versions[-1]` — the *newest* release the manifest doesn't list. When more than one release has been cut since the last backfill, the intermediate release(s) get no kept data at all, so hand-written fields are dropped or misattributed. Concrete case: the manifest has fragment `knob_added.foo.toml` with `why = "because reasons"`; between backfills, releases 0.2.4 and 0.2.5 are cut, and `foo` was added in 0.2.4 (untouched in 0.2.5). `assign_unreleased` moves the bucket to `0.2.5`; the history loop then computes 0.2.4's entry with `mine = kept.get("0.2.4", empty)` (empty), so `diff` regenerates `why` from `KNOB_DOCS`, and 0.2.5's diff has no `("knob_added","foo")` entry at all — the hand-written `why` is silently lost. Manual (`feature`/`refresh`/`repair`) entries have the same problem, and are worse: a feature actually introduced in 0.2.4 is emitted under 0.2.5's `[[release.change]]` sections, i.e. attributed to the wrong release. The docstring's "the newest release that the manifest does not list yet" only holds when exactly one release is unlisted.
chunk_findings.title: scripts/upgrade_manifest.py: assign_unreleased / backfill (the `kept.get(v, empty)` loop)

chunk_findings.detail: For a relative `--tree`, `PYTHONPATH` is set to the same relative string that is used as `cwd`, so Python resolves it against the new working directory. Input: `scripts/upgrade_manifest.py snapshot --tree ddflow` runs the child with `cwd=ddflow` and `PYTHONPATH=ddflow`, which resolves to `ddflow/ddflow` — nonexistent. So either the import fails (nonzero exit → `SystemExit`), or, when `ddflow` happens to be installed in the environment (the normal `uv run` case), the import silently succeeds from site-packages and the command prints the knobs/event kinds of the wrong tree instead of the requested one. The script's own callers are unaffected because they always pass absolute paths (`ROOT`, the extracted tmp dir), so this only breaks the documented `snapshot --tree DIR` entry point.

chunk_findings.detail: `release_key` assumes it is handed a parseable version — it returns `(0, version_key(version))` with no guard — and `parse` relies on that. Release versions are filtered through `version_key` beforehand (`if not version or (version != UNRELEASED and not version_key(version)): raise ManifestError`), but `base_version` is only checked for truthiness (`if not isinstance(base, dict) or not base.get("version")`). `parse` then calls `release_key(out.base_version)` when validating the ordering. Input: a manifest that otherwise satisfies the schema, e.g. `schema_version = 1` / `[base]` / `version = "main"` / `[[release]]` / `version = "0.2.0"` (or `[base] version = ["0.1.3"]`, which `str()` turns into `"['0.1.3']"`). `version_key("main")` is unparsable, and the explicit `else (0, ())` fallback in `changes_since` shows that an unparsable version does not produce a usable key, so `release_key("main")` evaluates to `(0, None)`; the subsequent comparison `order[0] <= release_key(out.base_version)` then raises `TypeError: '<=' not supported between instances of 'tuple' and 'NoneType'` instead of the `ManifestError` that `parse`'s docstring promises for a schema break (and if `version_key` returned an empty tuple instead of `None`, the invalid base version would be silently accepted, which is still not a `ManifestError`). The same unguarded call is reached in `replay`, where `limit = release_key(upto) if upto else None` feeds an unvalidated `upto` straight into `release_key(v) > limit`, so `replay(upto="main")` blows up on the first release rather than reporting an error. The fix for the earlier schema-validation finding covered only the `[[release]]` elements, not `base.version` or `upto`.

The sentence ends on an opening example marker `(e.g.` with no example and no closing parenthesis, so the user-facing explanation surfaced by `services/upgrade_manifest.changes_since("0.1.11")` (and the README section) is incomplete for anyone reading the 0.1.11→0.1.12 history. chunk_findings.detail:
`assign_unreleased` pops `UM.UNRELEASED` out of `kept`, hands its `by_key` to the versions cut since the last backfill, and never puts it back. Then `backfill` regenerates the new working-tree fragments with `mine = kept.get(UM.UNRELEASED, empty)` (`scripts/upgrade_manifest.py`, the `for e in diff(UM.UNRELEASED, ...)` loop), so the loose bucket is gone and the hand-written fields are replaced by the generated ones.

The result is silent loss whenever a release is cut that does *not* contain the fragment's key, while the change is still only in the working tree. Example: backfill once with no fragments; cut release 0.2.4 (a hotfix that does not contain the new `foo` knob); then add `foo` to the tree and write `unreleased/knob_added.foo.toml` with `why = "because reasons"`; run `backfill` again. `snaps` now ends at 0.2.4, so `unlisted = ["0.2.4"]`, `loose["by_key"]` (containing `("knob_added","foo") -> why="because reasons"`) is attached to 0.2.4 — whose `diff` does not contain `foo`, so it is unused — and `UNRELEASED` is removed from `kept`. The regenerated `unreleased/knob_added.foo.toml` is therefore written with `why = _why(doc)` (plus `impact = "additive"`), and the file on disk overwrites the hand-written `why`. The `assign_unreleased` docstring promises the fragment's fields "serve every release the manifest does not list yet", but the newly regenerated unreleased entry is exactly such a version and it does not receive them. The fixes/probes for the earlier finding only assert that a *cut* release whose diff contains the key picks the fields up; they do not cover the key that is absent from every cut, and the not-yet-cut entry is still dropped. The loss is silent: no error, just a generic `why` in the next manifest.
chunk_findings.title: scripts/upgrade_manifest.py:assign_unreleased / backfill

chunk_findings.detail: The base snapshot validates `[base.knobs]` (`isinstance(raw_knobs, dict)`) but leaves `event_kinds` completely unchecked: `sorted(base.get("event_kinds") or [])`. An `event_kinds` value that is not a list of strings is therefore either silently mis-parsed or escapes as a raw exception. Concretely, a manifest written with `event_kinds = "handoff"` (a string instead of `event_kinds = ["handoff"]`) parses to the six phantom kinds `['a','d','f','h','n','o']`, and `base.get("event_kinds")` being a table `[base.event_kinds]` yields the table's keys as the base event vocabulary; `replay()`/`changes_since()` then report these phantom base kinds. Worse, a scalar such as `event_kinds = 5` makes `sorted(5)` raise `TypeError`, which is not the `ManifestError` the function's contract promises, so callers that catch `ManifestError` (the documented failure mode) crash instead. This is the same unvalidated-shape hole that was fixed for `[base.knobs]`, left open for the sibling field; adding an `isinstance(..., list)` (and element) check, mirroring the knobs check, closes it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_manifest.py:parse

chunk_findings.detail: The `why` value for the newly added knob `flow.version_files` is truncated mid-sentence: `"Files \`version cut\` bumps, as path -> regex with exactly ONE capture group, the version text (e.g."`. It terminates in a dangling `(e.g.` with no example and no closing parenthesis. A user upgrading to 0.1.12 and reading this entry (or a consumer of `services/upgrade_manifest.changes_since(version)` that surfaces `why`) gets an incomplete explanation of a knob whose whole point is the exact one-capture-group regex format — the example is precisely the part that teaches the format. This is the same class of defect as the two triaged truncations, but the probe the author used (`grep -c '\.\.\.\"$'`) only catches values ending in `...`; this value ends in `(e.g.`, so it was never detected or fixed. Note it is only ~99 characters, well under the 240-char cap the author blamed, so it is a hand-written incomplete value rather than a cap-truncation. Every other `why` in the file (including the two fixed ones) is a complete sentence; this is the sole exception.

chunk_findings.detail: `match` carefully wraps `regex(...)` in `try/except re.error` so that a pattern git accepts but Python cannot compile "matches only itself, never crashes a claim or a commit". But `inside` and `overlap` do not go through `match` for their fast paths — they call `fnmatch.fnmatch` directly (`inside` at the first condition, `overlap` in `if fnmatch(a, b) or fnmatch(b, a)`), and `fnmatch` compiles the pattern with `re` internally and does *not* swallow errors. The descending-class-range case the module docstring itself names as the motivating example therefore escapes uncaught: `inside("a.md", "[z-a]")` or `overlap("[z-a]", "src/*.md")` raises `re.error: bad character range z-a` instead of returning a bool. Since the module docstring says these two functions are what "the lease conflict detector asks", a claim/glob of `[z-a]` (which git reads, per that same docstring) crashes the conflict detector — the exact failure the `match` guard was written to prevent, and which `overlap` is additionally documented as being "built on the same translator" although it never calls it. Wrapping the `fnmatch` calls in the same `except re.error` (e.g. reuse `match`) removes the crash.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/globs.py:inside / overlap (the `fnmatch` calls)

chunk_findings.detail: The removed `path_in_glob` was not a plain git matcher: its own docstring records that it deliberately deviated from git for two cases, because claims written in this codebase depend on the deviation. First, for a pattern with no `/` it stopped after `fnmatch` and returned `False` ("git would match a bare name at any depth; a claim on `a.md` is one file"). Second, it relied on `fnmatch`, "whose `*` crosses `/`, as the claims written so far assume". The Intent of this change states that `core/globs.inside` is a *git* reading of patterns, and git does the opposite on both points: a slash-less pattern matches the basename at any depth, and `*` does not cross `/`. Concretely, `path_in_glob("src/a.md", "a.md")` now returns `True` where the deleted code documented it must return `False` (a claim on `a.md` is one file), and `path_in_glob("src/a/b.py", "src/*.py")` now returns `False` where the deleted code returned `True`. If any caller still treats a claim glob as covering exactly the named file, or relies on `*` spanning directories (the case the old docstring says claims were written for), it will now compute coverage/overlap backwards — e.g. a lease on `a.md` will be treated as covering `docs/a.md`, and a lease on `src/*.py` will no longer cover `src/pkg/mod.py`. This is only safe if `globs.inside` re-implements the bare-name special case and the fnmatch-style `*`; the visible diff provides no such guarantee, and the new module is described as git-faithful.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/schedule.py:27 (re-export `from .globs import inside as path_in_glob`)

chunk_findings.detail: The rewrite drops the explicit `glob == s` short-circuit that the old body had (`if glob == s or _gitattributes_re(s).match(glob): return True`). It now relies entirely on `glob_match(...)` matching the claim's glob — which is itself a *pattern*, not a concrete path — against the shared pattern. Any shared glob that contains a character class does not match its own source text, because `[ab]` only matches the characters `a`/`b` (and `[!a]`/`[^a]` only match anything-but-`a`), never the literal `[`. So for input `is_shared("[ab].md", ["[ab].md"])` the matcher is asked to match the path string `[ab].md` against the class pattern `[ab].md`; position 0 requires `a`, `b` (or a non-`a` for the negated form) but the subject has `[`, and since the pattern is anchored at the start the match fails and `is_shared` returns `False`. Previously the equality clause (and, incidentally, the `_class_end` handling that made `[]]`, `[^]]`, `[!...]` valid) returned `True`. The same failure occurs for any claim whose glob is byte-identical to a shared glob but contains `[`/`[!`/`[^`, i.e. exactly the patterns the removed `_class_end`/`body.startswith("!")` code was written to support. The consequence is that a claim sharing a file by an identical class-bearing glob is no longer recognised as shared, so it is treated as exclusive and can conflict with the other claim/merge path that git *does* consider shared (git's `.gitattributes` reads the class and would union-merge it). The old behaviour was pinned by tests (the docstring explicitly touted `[]]`/`[^]]`), and nothing in the new call replaces the identity case.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/schedule.py (is_shared, the new `return any(glob_match(glob, s, ...) ...)`)

chunk_findings.detail: `is_doc` was converted from `glob_regex(g).fullmatch(path)` to `any(globs.match(path, g) for g in doc_globs)` without passing `bare_any_depth=True`, while `inventory.py:104` passes it for the same "doc glob" semantics. With any bare pattern (e.g. `doc_globs = ["*.md"]`), `globs.match("guides/a.md", "*.md")` compares `*.md` with `/`‑crossing disabled and returns False, whereas git pathspecs match a slash‑less pattern against the basename at any depth (and inventory does match it). So `is_doc("guides/a.md", ["*.md"])` is False while the identical glob selects that file in inventory: the doc set used by `git grep`/doc sync and the doc set used elsewhere disagree, and the stated bug fix "doc globs now read as git does" is not actually delivered for bare patterns. The call needs the same opt‑in the other doc‑glob caller uses.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docsync.py:is_doc

chunk_findings.detail: The archive check was changed from `fnmatch.fnmatch(rel, g)` (where `*` crosses `/`, so `fnmatch("lessons/archive/old.md", "*.md")` is True) to `glob_match(rel, g)` with no `bare_any_depth`. With a slash‑less archive glob such as `*.md` or `old.md`, `glob_match("lessons/archive/old.md", "*.md")` now returns False, so a file that was previously marked archived (and which git would also match) is treated as an active, non‑archived section, changing phase/blocking behavior. Since `inventory.py` explicitly requests `bare_any_depth=True` for the same kind of conversion, this call is inconsistent with the intended git semantics.

chunk_findings.detail: The property `globs.match(glob, glob) is True` is false for any glob containing a valid character class, and the Hypothesis strategy `_glob` can generate exactly such a glob. `_ALPHA` contains `"[ab]"`, so `_glob` yields the pattern `"[ab]"` (and many like `"docs[ab]"`, `".md[ab]"`). The table this same file pins (`("a[0-9].md", "a5.md", True, True)`) establishes that classes are compiled as classes, not as literals; only patterns Python's `re` cannot compile (e.g. `"a[z-a]"`) fall back to literal matching, which is what `test_a_pattern_git_reads_and_python_cannot_matches_only_itself` covers. Therefore for `glob="[ab]"`, `path="[ab]"` the pattern matches a single character `a` or `b`, while the path is the four characters `[`, `a`, `b`, `]`, so `globs.match("[ab]", "[ab]")` returns `False` and the assertion fails. Since `"[ab]"` is directly in the sampling set, Hypothesis will find (and shrink to) it immediately, so the test suite added by this change cannot pass as written.

chunk_findings.detail: `inside` evaluates `fnmatch(path, glob)` as an un-guarded disjunct. Given `glob = "[z-a]"` (a descending class range — precisely the pattern the module docstring says `regex` must raise on) and any `path` that is not literally `"[z-a]"` and does not start with `"[z-a]/"`, e.g. `inside("a", "[z-a]")`: the first two conditions are `False`, so `fnmatch("a", "[z-a]")` runs; `fnmatch.translate` emits `[z-a]` and `re.compile` raises `re.error: bad character range z-a`. The exception escapes `inside`, contradicting "never crashes a claim"; `match()`'s `try/except` is never reached because `fnmatch` is called first. The same happens for any other git-readable-but-Python-invalid class (e.g. `[a-\]`).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/globs.py:inside

chunk_findings.detail: `overlap` calls `fnmatch(a, b)` / `fnmatch(b, a)` with the raw patterns and no error guard. `overlap("a", "[z-a]")`: `a != b`, so `fnmatch("a", "[z-a]")` compiles the pattern `[z-a]` and raises `re.error: bad character range z-a`, escaping the function. A single lease/`shared_globs` line containing a descending range therefore crashes the conflict detector that `overlap` feeds, even though the module claims such patterns are handled ("matches only itself").
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/globs.py:overlap

chunk_findings.detail: The hunk deletes `import functools` and `import re`, but neither of the two functions being deleted (`globs_overlap`, `path_in_glob`) uses `functools` at all, and only `path_in_glob` touches `re` (for `re.error`). That means `functools` (and almost certainly `re`, via the compiled-regex helper `_gitattributes_re` that the deleted `path_in_glob` called) is still referenced by code that this diff does not remove. Concretely: if `_gitattributes_re` remains defined in `schedule.py` as a regex-compiling helper (which it must be, since the new `.globs` module is only added in this change set and the imports added here name only `inside`/`match`/`overlap`), then the deleted `path_in_glob`'s call `_gitattributes_re(glob).match(path)` had a surviving definition whose body uses `re.compile` — and if it is decorated with `@functools.lru_cache`/`functools.cache`, module import raises `NameError: name 'functools' is not defined` for `ddflow.core.schedule`, breaking every importer (flow, docsync, inventory, CLI). If the decorator isn't used, the failure is deferred to the first call into `_gitattributes_re`, again surfacing as `NameError` rather than the intended glob result. Removing an import that was never used by the deleted code is only safe if the same commit also saved/removed `_gitattributes_re`; that removal is not present in this part of the diff. Verify `_gitattributes_re` (and any `re.`/`functools.` use elsewhere in `schedule.py`) before accepting.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/schedule.py: imports (removed `import functools` / `import re`)

chunk_findings.detail: The old body tested `glob == s` before attempting a pattern match, and the removed helper's docstring records why that fallback matters ("a pattern git would read and we cannot: equality only, never a crash"). The new body drops this identity short-circuit and relies solely on `glob_match(glob, s, bare_any_depth=True)`, which is a path-vs-pattern matcher and therefore cannot match a literal string containing glob metacharacters against itself. Concrete input: `shared = ["[abc].txt"]`, `glob = "[abc].txt"`. The old code returned `True` because `glob == s`; the new code asks the matcher whether the literal path `[abc].txt` matches the pattern `[abc].txt`, where `[abc]` is a one-character class, so the leading `[` does not match and it returns `False`. The same regression hits any shared entry containing a bracket class that is also the claim glob/path (e.g. a file named `foo[1].txt`, or the `[^]]`-style patterns the removed `_class_end` docstring was specifically about). `is_shared` then reports the item as not shared, so it is treated as exclusive and conflict resolution differs from the behaviour these tests were supposed to pin.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/schedule.py:is_shared (rewritten return line)

chunk_findings.detail:
`bare_any_depth=True` makes a slash-less glob match at any depth, which reproduces `fnmatch.fnmatch` for patterns like `*.py`. It does **not** reproduce `fnmatch`'s other two differences: in `fnmatch`, `*` crosses `/` and `?` matches `/`. Any pattern that contains a literal `/` (so the any-depth prefix is not applied) is therefore interpreted with git-glob semantics where `*`/`?` stop at `/`, whereas the old code let them cross it.

Concrete regression: with an inventory/archive glob of `docs/*.md`, the old `fnmatch(rel, "docs/*.md")` matched `docs/sub/notes.md` (the `*` consumed `sub/notes`) and the file was included/archived. After the change, `glob_match("docs/sub/notes.md", "docs/*.md", bare_any_depth=True)` reduces to `docs/[^/]*\.md` fullmatch, which fails because `*` no longer crosses the extra `/`; the file is silently dropped from the inventory result (and, in the importer, the section is no longer marked archived/held). Likewise `fnmatch("a/b", "a?b")` was `True` (`?` matched `/`), but with `bare_any_depth=True` a bare pattern `a?b` becomes `**/a[^/]b`, which does not match `a/b`. If the intent is to preserve the behaviour the old tests pinned for these two call sites, the compatibility layer needs to also let `*`/`?` cross `/` (or the call sites need to stop using `fnmatch`-era globs).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/inventory.py:104 and ddflow/services/importer.py:903

chunk_findings.detail: The property asserts that any generated pattern matches its own literal text, but the strategy `_ALPHA` includes the token `"[ab]"`, and the same file documents (row `("a[0-9].md", "a5.md", True, True)`, `("a[!0-9].md", "a5.md", False, False)`, `("a[^0-9].md", "ax.md", True, True)`, and the new `docs/[ab].md` test) that `[...]` is a character class, not literal text. Hypothesis will therefore reach `_glob == "[ab]"` and evaluate `globs.match("[ab]", "[ab]")`: the translated pattern is the one-character class (`re.fullmatch(r"[ab]\Z", "[ab]")` is `None`, since `"[ab]"` is four characters and contains neither `a` nor `b`), so the call returns `False` and the assertion fails. The `a[z-a]` case in `test_a_pattern_git_reads_and_python_cannot_matches_only_itself` does not save this: that pattern only yields `True` because `re.compile("[z-a]")` raises and the implementation falls back to literal comparison, whereas `[ab]` compiles cleanly as a class. Note also that a git-faithful matcher must return `False` here (git's wildmatch treats `[ab]` as a class), so if the "equality" property instead holds, the implementation is carrying an undocumented `path == pattern` shortcut that diverges from the stated "git reading of patterns" for every class pattern. Either way the test encodes a false invariant and will not pass against a correct implementation.

chunk_findings.detail: `overlap` never normalizes a leading `/`, even though `regex` explicitly lstrip`s it and the module documents "a leading `/` anchors". An anchored pattern and its unanchored equivalent therefore denote the same path for `match`/`inside` but are reported as non-overlapping. Concrete: `overlap("/src/a.md", "src/a.md")` goes through `fnmatch("/src/a.md","src/a.md")` (literal, `False`) and `fnmatch("src/a.md","/src/a.md")` (literal, `False`), then `pa="/src/a.md"`, `pb="src/a.md"`: neither `pa.startswith(pb)` nor `pb.startswith(pa)` (the leading slash), so it returns `False`. But `match("src/a.md", "/src/a.md")` is `True` (regex strips the `/`, `anchored` is `True`, pattern becomes `src/a\.md\Z`) and `match("src/a.md", "src/a.md")` is `True`, i.e. the two patterns demonstrably cover the same file. The same happens for e.g. `overlap("/src/a.md", "src/*.md")`. Since `overlap` is one of the two questions the lease conflict detector asks ("could two claims share a file"), this false negative can let two claims on the same path be treated as disjoint (no re-order/serialization), which is the class of bug the `inside` docstring cites (`B1997c64c5a`). The prefix heuristic should compare prefixes after stripping a leading `/` (and, for consistency, `fnmatch` should be fed the same normalized form).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/globs.py:overlap (the `pa`/`pb` literal-prefix comparison)

chunk_findings.detail: `archived = any(glob_match(rel, g) for g in archive)` drops the `bare_any_depth=True` flag that the pre-change `fnmatch.fnmatch(rel, g)` implicitly provided for slash-less patterns. `globs.match` defaults to `bare_any_depth=False` — that is exactly why `docsync.is_doc` (which relies on the default, and whose earlier finding was refuted on the ground that its old translator anchored bare names at the root) and `inventory.py` (which explicitly passes `bare_any_depth=True` to keep the old lenient reading) call it the two different ways. With an archive glob of `*.md`, the old code matched `lessons/archive/old.md` (`*` crosses `/`), whereas `glob_match("lessons/archive/old.md", "*.md")` with the default is `False`, so a section the operator intended to archive is treated as active, changing phase/blocking behavior. The triage marks finding 5 `confirmed` and points at `tests/test_globs.py::test_importer_archive_globs_use_the_same_reading (bare_any_depth)`, but the diff at this line still omits the flag; the probe only pins the bare-any-depth reading for `inventory.py:104`, not this call site. The fix is to pass `bare_any_depth=True` here as `inventory.py` does.

chunk_findings.detail: `overlap` never normalizes a leading `/`, even though `regex` explicitly lstrip`s it and the module documents "a leading `/` anchors". An anchored pattern and its unanchored equivalent therefore denote the same path for `match`/`inside` but are reported as non-overlapping. Concrete: `overlap("/src/a.md", "src/a.md")` goes through `fnmatch("/src/a.md","src/a.md")` (literal, `False`) and `fnmatch("src/a.md","/src/a.md")` (literal, `False`), then `pa="/src/a.md"`, `pb="src/a.md"`: neither `pa.startswith(pb)` nor `pb.startswith(pa)` (the leading slash), so it returns `False`. But `match("src/a.md", "/src/a.md")` is `True` (regex strips the `/`, `anchored` is `True`, pattern becomes `src/a\.md\Z`) and `match("src/a.md", "src/a.md")` is `True`, i.e. the two patterns demonstrably cover the same file. The same happens for e.g. `overlap("/src/a.md", "src/*.md")`. Since `overlap` is one of the two questions the lease conflict detector asks ("could two claims share a file"), this false negative can let two claims on the same path be treated as disjoint (no re-order/serialization), which is the class of bug the `inside` docstring cites (`B1997c64c5a`). The prefix heuristic should compare prefixes after stripping a leading `/` (and, for consistency, `fnmatch` should be fed the same normalized form).
